speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. Si. Laurent (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: EXTENSION OF GOOD WISHES TO CANADIAN
subsubtopic: DELEGATES TO FORTHCOMING MEETING
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I take a moment or two at this time to express on behalf of all the members of the official opposition our good wishes to the Prime Minister and his colleagues the Minister of Finance and the Minister of National Defence who, I believe, will be leaving early this evening to attend the extraordinary council meeting of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization in Paris next week. I can assure the Prime Minister and his colleagues that these good wishes are very sincere and I have no doubt that they are shared by every member of this house-

subtopic: EXTENSION OF GOOD WISHES TO CANADIAN
subsubtopic: DELEGATES TO FORTHCOMING MEETING
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: EXTENSION OF GOOD WISHES TO CANADIAN
subsubtopic: DELEGATES TO FORTHCOMING MEETING
speechtext:
-regardless of party affiliations and generally by the people of Canada.
Of course these good wishes extend also to the Secretary of State for External Affairs who, I understand, had to leave a little earlier and who by this time has probably already reached his first destination.
Naturally these good wishes include the very hearty and confident hopes that the Prime Minister and the members of his party will have a comfortable and safe journey and will be back in our midst at the time fixed in their schedule. Those personal wishes come from the esteem and friendship which the members of this house have for the Prime Minister and his colleagues who will be representing Canada on this important occasion.
We all realize, of course, how important to the members of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization is this special meeting and, as the Prime Minister reminded the house
on Wednesday in the exchange of questions and answers recorded in Hansard of that day, the character of the meeting probably arises from the earlier meeting of the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom and the President of the United States a few weeks ago. The Prime Minister added:
It also arises from the realization that the recent scientific advances on the part of the U.S.S.R. have called for an intensified examination of NATO and its principles, to the end that it may advance to the future stronger than ever before in its purposes and in its aims.
There are, no doubt, many difficult and complex problems which will be the object of consideration at this meeting. We understand the heads of the governments of most of the member countries will be present. I am not going to refer any more to these difficulties, because that would not serve any useful purpose at this time, but we have had an example of their number and complexity in these exchanges which have taken place from time to time in the House of Commons, and the Prime Minister said on Wednesday that as to the furtherance and extension of the application of article 2 of the North Atlantic treaty he felt he would be speaking with the approval of the members of the house.
I think I can say in a general but very sincere way that the Prime Minister may feel that he and his colleagues will have behind them the support of all the members of this house and of the public generally in their efforts to promote what has been the usual attitude of Canada as a middle power in its endeavours to smooth out the disagreements which are bound to arise from time to time between the leaders of countries engaged in a common pursuit, disagreements which are certainly overweighed by the general desire of all the members of the organization, their governments and peoples, to promote and try to secure peace in the world.
They will be doing this at a time when we are all reminded of the age-old promise of peace in the world to men of good will.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF GOOD WISHES TO CANADIAN
subsubtopic: DELEGATES TO FORTHCOMING MEETING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I join the Leader of the Opposition in expressing good wishes to the Prime Minister and the members of his party who are attending this very important conference in Paris. There are times when party differences are put aside and we can be unanimous

NATO-Paris Conference in our good wishes, and this is especially so in connection with a conference of this nature.
I think in all probability this organization has never met with the eyes of so many people upon it as at the present time. I was very glad to hear the Secretary of State for External Affairs say the other day that some way must be found of negotiating with those with whom we have been at variance over the years in order that the world may be protected from the threat of destruction which has been hanging over it for so long.
The North Atlantic Treaty Organization, I remember well, was first suggested at the United Nations by the Leader of the Opposition. I was a member of the Canadian delegation when that proposal was made at the United Nations assembly in 1946, and there is one feature of it which I hope the Prime Minister and his colleagues will stress, namely article 2, for economic co-operation. I believe more can be done to unite the western nations by article 2 than by any other means.
All we hope is that our delegation will be able to promote peace among the nations of the world, and I can assure the Prime Minister that we wish him and the delegation every success in the great undertaking in which they will be engaged next week. I know, as the Leader of the Opposition has said, that this feeling is shared not only by everyone in this House of Commons but by the people in every part of Canada.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF GOOD WISHES TO CANADIAN
subsubtopic: DELEGATES TO FORTHCOMING MEETING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure it will not require a multiplication of words to add my good wishes to the expressions of good will which the Prime Minister and his colleagues have received from all sides of the house on leaving to take part in this summit conference in Paris. I can only say that those speakers who have preceded me spoke words which are in my own heart and mind.
I should also like to say that the circumstances at this time are unusual. These are dangerous times, and it seems to me they will require an unusual amount of co-operation among the nations which are now called the free nations of the world. If this NATO meeting can result in an extension of the application of article 2 in such a manner as to bring about this unusual measure of cooperation, I think we can see some life at the other end of the tunnel. I believe representatives of the nations attending this meeting must go to unusual lengths in seeking ways of removing fear, because I believe that today fear is the greatest cause of world tension.

I believe the place to start is with ourselves and the way we work with other nations and treat other nations. I also believe that there is more reason today to play the game with the utmost honesty, in the first place, than ever before and if our delegation can give leadership at the NATO conference in that respect and on a high moral plane I am satisfied the results will be good. Our best wishes go with them.
Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime
Minister): Mr. Speaker, I need not say how deeply grateful I am to have the expression of the viewpoint of the right hon. Leader of the Opposition and the leaders of the C.C.F. and Social Credit parties. This is one of those times when in a spirit of unity the House of Commons demonstrates the true relationship between members of various political parties that is of the essence of parliamentary government and the preservation of freedom as we see it. Indeed, what has been said here this morning is indicative of the strength of our system, which permits strong and definite opinions being expressed regarding those matters which separate us while at the same time maintaining not only the amenities but the friendships that exist among those who although they represent different viewpoints are united in their common dedication to the worth-while things of life.
As I speak for my colleagues and myself, may I say how much what has been said here today will mean to us in the days that are ahead as we meet with the representatives of the other 14 countries composing NATO, not in an aggressive attitude, not in a belligerent attitude, but in a realization that only in the maintenance of our undivided unity and in dissolving those things that separate us from time to time will freedom truly be preserved.
When reference was made to the fact that the Leader of the Opposition first raised this question of unity in the free world it brought to me a feeling of pride as a Canadian that the idea and concept should have been first introduced at an international meeting by one of those within this parliament who still occupies a high position in the deliberations of our country. There is no one, I am sure, who realizes more than I that in recent months, indeed in the last year and a half or two years, certain profound differences have arisen among members of NATO.
There is nothing unhealthy or abnormal in that fact. Communist countries are able to deny the beneficial effect of criticism or disagreement. We know there have been difficulties and disagreements, and my hope is that this conference, playing as it does an important role in providing a forum for consultation, will achieve that unity of purpose

to which I have already alluded, that rededication to principles upon which NATO had its beginnings, the redeclaration of its aims and purposes, so that we shall be able among the forces of freedom to advance into the sombre days of the future once again realizing that we have established a unity beneficial to the maintenance of peace. Indeed, without it peace cannot be assured.
We should not exaggerate our difficulties nor our problems. That we can meet at this time and that the heads of the various states will be able to meet indicates that the alliance retains its basic strength and vitality, that its principles still retain a basic similarity of point of view.
There is one thing that I think we must make clear, and that has been made clear this morning. NATO has no aggressive purpose. Mention was made of the need to dissipate fear in the world as a major element in preserving peace. At this meeting I hope it will again be made abundantly clear that this is a defence alliance; that the basic purpose of NATO is to deter aggression and to preserve peace. That is the attitude of this parliament as I see it today.
A prime minister's responsibility, and the responsibility of those associated with him, must always be so to speak as to convey to other nations what has been the traditional position of Canada, a middle power exerting its influence, as the Leader of the Opposition said, among other nations joined with us who have their disagreements-disagreements which are natural-and do those things which we believe are necessary.
My hope is that out of this NATO meeting will come that new spirit which is expected not only by the peoples of the free world, but also by men and women of good will everywhere. Our purpose will be to make the contribution, however small, that is available to us to bring about the achievement of what the Leader of the Opposition said, peace on earth to men of good will.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, some days ago the hon. member for Peace River asked for a report on the progress of P.F.A. inspections in the Peace river area, where disastrous crop conditions exist. Yesterday he asked the Prime Minister whether the government would make a full investigation. I think I should point out that the investigation currently being carried on, as will become clear when I make this statement, is perhaps as thorough an investigation into what the crop conditions are as could possibly be made.
Inspections are being carried out in the Peace river country and Athabasca districts of Alberta as speedily as possible, but the work is being delayed by extremely bad weather. In the Peace river area on December 9 there were 25 field inspectors working, and supervisory officers were contacting as many other qualified men as are available with a view to getting the inspection work completed in as short a time as possible. I might say we hope to have 50 men at work as soon as they can be secured, given their training and put into the field.
Checking offices have been opened at Sex-smith and Falher, and clerks have been hired to help process returns as they come in. A third office may be opened in the town of Peace River. It has been reported that four inches of snow and rain fell on December 8 and that road conditions are extremely bad, which is delaying the work. In several districts the inspectors can get around only on horseback.
Because of the bad weather and the inability of the field inspectors to report promptly, it is not possible to say how much of the work has been done to date. However, a close check is being kept and the supervisory officials who have been sent to the area are doing all they can to avoid any delays.


The hon. member for Athabasca said to me yesterday that the same conditions prevail there as in the Peace river country. I promised him that I would investigate that matter, and I have a report on it. In the Athabasca district about 70 townships have been applied for, and inspections are almost completed. While harvesting has been delayed in some parts by the weather, the situation does not compare with that in Peace river. There appears to be a problem in about ten townships, and the municipality of St. Paul has asked to meet with the district supervisor. A meeting has been arranged for December 16.
It appears that in this district, as in several others, there are some unthreshed crops that are salvageable; that is, it will be possible to thresh them this winter or in the spring. In such cases the inspection work will not be undertaken until harvesting is completed. In most of the Peace river area the unthreshed crops remaining in the fields are definitely not salvageable.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to address a question to the Minister of Labour. I am sorry I was not able to give him notice until after coming into the house. Has the Minister of Labour received a further request on behalf of the salmon gill net and seine fishermen of British Columbia who are faced with a problem in connection with unemployment insurance because they have fewer than 15 contributions? If so, can he tell the house what steps are being taken by him or by the unemployment insurance commission to deal with the serious problem being faced by these fishermen?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: REQUEST FOR EMERGENCY REGULATION TO COVER PACIFIC COAST FISHERMEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in answer to the hon. member's question I wish to say that I have received representations from the united fishermen and allied workers' union in British Columbia as well as other representations with regard to relaxing the seasonal provisions of the unemployment insurance regulations further so that fishermen with fewer than 15 stamps might receive seasonal benefits.
This matter has been given very careful study with my officials, and the decision is that I do not feel a further relaxation of these provisions would be in order at this time. I am sure it will be appreciated that a relaxation of the requirements on behalf of one particular group would soon result in

demands from other groups and individuals for a similar relaxation. To meet this demand would entail a further revision of the seasonal benefit regulations which have just recently been revised to provide a longer benefit season. Thus I am afraid I cannot see my way clear to recommend the further relaxation which has been requested in this case.

speechtext: The house resumed, from December 12, 1957, consideration of the motion of Mr. Fleming for the second reading of Bill No. 232, to amend the Income Tax Act.

Mr. Speaker, when I moved the adjournment of this debate last night I was pointing out that the proposed amendments to the Income Tax Act still leave that act as one which taxes some of those who should not be taxed and fails to tax some of those who should be taxed, with the result that we do not have sufficient revenue to provide sound taxation policies which would be fair to all people in Canada.
In particular, the amendments fail to do enough in the way of exemptions for children. Naturally I welcome the extension of the exemption in the case of dependent children from $150 to $250, but I think hon. members will agree that this is not nearly enough in view of the cost of living and, in particular, the cost of raising a child in the world today. I agree, too-and I think this statement was made by the hon. member for Montmagny-L'Islet (Mr. Lesage) last night- that the better course to pursue would undoubtedly be to improve family allowances. I say that partly because we know that increasing income tax exemptions in respect of dependent children does not help those many Canadians who do not pay income tax at all. I say it also because too often in my law practice I have had experience with cases where it was most important that something be given to the mother in the family, as is the family allowance, rather than to the father because in broken homes or nearly broken homes, due to alcoholism or some other factor, the breadwinner was not capable of looking after his own family. The principle adopted under the family allowance regulations of sending the cheque directly to the mother is a beneficent one, and I regret that the government has not seen fit to improve family allowance at the present time.
In addition, of course, the present act, as I pointed out last night, does not begin to meet the legitimate expectations of the

Canadian people for an increase in the amount of personal exemptions.
What are the proposals I have to make with a view to alternative revenues; because if we are going to increase personal exemptions and give a better break to the children of Canada, to give every one of them an equal chance of recreation, health, housing and educational advantages, where are we to find the alternative revenues? I wish to draw attention to three cases where we are failing to tax those who should be taxed, cases where special privilege is still enshrined as a principle in our income tax legislation.
The first I will deal with briefly, because it has already been dealt with in this house; that is, the iniquitous 2 per cent tax for the old age security fund. That 2 per cent, as hon. members of this house know, applies only upon the first $3,000 of taxable income; so the situation arises-and I say it is an iniquitous situation-where a man with $3,000 of taxable income pays $60; a man with $30,000 of taxable income pays the same sum, $60, and a man with $300,000 of taxable income still pays $60 only.
This is special privilege with a vengeance, and it is also poor husbandry on the part of the government, because there is an additional source of revenue were that 2 per cent not only to be extended throughout all income tax brackets but graduated, as it should be, to fall more heavily on large incomes.
The next example I wish to refer to is the privilege-I call it the special privilege- conferred under section 38 of the Income Tax Act; that is, the privilege of deducting from taxation 20 per cent of all dividends received from Canadian companies. This situation, grotesque in terms of fair taxation, was presented to the house by the hon. member for Nanaimo speaking on March 12 of this year, and I want to give the house again the example he then presented to the former minister of finance. I am referring to page 2471 of Hansard for 1957.
Here, as the hon. member pointed out, you can consider two cases, each concerning married men with no children. Each has a gross income of $11,133. In the case of the man who gets that $11,133 in dividends from Canadian companies, his income tax would be $1,877.24 before the rebate is given, plus a surtax of 4 per cent on investment income over $2,400, or $349, making the total tax $2,226.56. That man would get a tax credit of 20 per cent of $11,133, his gross income, which would amount to $2,226.60.
In the case of this unearned income, that special credit under section 38 entirely wipes out his tax and $60 only is paid into the old
Income Tax Act
age security fund. In the case of the man who earns the income, he pays his full tax of $1,877.24.
With all deference, Mr. Speaker, I submit that this is discrimination which still exists in our income tax legislation. It is a case where we are extending favours to income that comes from owning, not doing. We are extending a special favour to income that is begotten by wealth, not service, when in all fairness and simple justice it should of course be the other way around.
The next section to which I wish to turn for my third point is section 8, subsection 1 of the Income Tax Act. The general section provides that any income conferred upon a shareholder of a corporation is of course taxable, but the exception is this. Any advantage of benefit conferred on a shareholder is not taxable when it confers "on all holders of common shares in the capital of the corporation a right to buy additional common shares therein."
What are some of the consequences that flow from those very few words? Already in this session of parliament we have given attention to two bills, one to increase the capitalization of the British Columbia Telephone Company from $75 million to $150 million and the other the Bell Telephone Company bill. I am referring to these merely as examples of the millions of dollars which go completely untaxed in this country because of that particular little section. In the case of the British Columbia Telephone Company the spokesman for that company stated quite frankly in committee that their increased capitalization would be issued in the form of share rights. They said they had always followed that procedure, and with the approval of the board of transport commissioners they intended to follow it in the future. In other words they will grant to their existing shareholders the right to purchase the new stock issued at six or eight points below the market, as the spokesman said. Income Tax Act

Mr. Speaker, with all deference may I state that my position is that we cannot weigh the advisability of approving the particular proposals with respect to revenues advanced by the government without considering alternative proposals.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
It is my view that the hon. member is out of order in discussing all the other provisions of the Income Tax Act which are not under review or subject to amendment in this bill. I would refer to a ruling of the Speaker in 1949 on that subject, to be found in the Journals of the House of Commons of the second session of 1949 at page 237, which reads:
On the second reading of an amending bill-it is the principle of the amending bill and not the principle of the act to be amended, which is the "business under consideration". The discussion must therefore relate exclusively to the principle of the amending bill.
As I say, I allowed a certain amount of discussion of the principle of income tax which is proposed to be modified, but it seems to me that the hon. member is going out into other forms and aspects of taxation which are not before us.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to abide by your ruling though with regret, not quarrelling so much with the ruling, which of course I cannot and do not do, as with the manner in which the government has introduced these changes, which perhaps has already been the subject of enough debate and rulings in this house and I will not refer further to it.
In order that my remarks already on the record will make some sense, I will conclude by saying that I regret that the government has not opened up section 8 of the Income Tax Act, because I believe that many millions of dollars now accruing to Canadians as unearned income could and should be the subject of income tax legislation.

statement I made that would undertake to override the rules of debate. What I said was that we would have a full opportunity to discuss the measures. is perfectly true that the Minister of Finance did not say he was asking the house to set aside its rules, but I think it is known that there are times when suggestions like this are made, and it is assumed that unanimous consent has been given if there is no objection. The house operates that way on many occasions. If the house misunderstood the meaning of the Minister of Finance last Friday I suppose that is unfortunate, but it did seem to me that what the minister was saying at that time was that we should not worry about the loss of the eight-day budget debate because we would have an opportunity to discuss these matters. He did not use these words at that point, but somewhere he used the words "to their heart's content".
Where do we get that opportunity if we do not get it on the second reading of so general a bill as the bill to amend the

Income Tax Act? For example, when we get into committee on this bill there is no question but that we are then limited strictly to the clauses of the bill, but at this point it would seem to me that you might continue to allow reasonable latitude.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I do propose to allow reasonable latitude. As the hon. member has pointed out, I consider that general remarks and arguments about what other taxation reductions might have been undertaken, other than those which are in this bill, are a proper subject of discussion, in view of the way in which these matters come before the house; but the reason I rose was that the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway was getting into discussion of specific sections of the Income Tax Act which are unaffected by this bill. I do not want to preclude him from discussing income tax in principle in connection with this bill, as I did not interfere with other members doing that before, but it is a question of becoming too specific. If hon. members will endeavour to hold the balance there I shall not try to restrict them unduly.

Mr. Speaker, I will proceed and try not to trespass on your patience or your ruling. I shall try to speak in a very general way and bring my remarks to a conclusion.
The point I was making about share rights was simply this. That is a general way of financing private expansions in corporate financing. It results in great increments to the shareholders of the companies concerned. Sometimes they can realize that benefit by retaining the shares which are given to them at below the market price; sometimes they can realize the benefit by selling the share rights; but however it may be done, it is a source of great benefit to a relatively small group of Canadians, which is totally untaxed at the present time.
I am going to conclude now, Mr. Speaker, by requesting all members, when they consider these specific amendments that are being proposed by the government, to ponder seriously whether the government has gone nearly far enough. I would appeal particularly to the members of the Liberal party to my right when these questions come up, such as the allowance to construction workers which is not going to be given to loggers at the present time, such as the adequacy of the exemptions for children, to speak as they think and to vote as they speak. I appeal to the government to consider trying to embody in the Income Tax Act what Shakespeare called "this even-handed justice". I ask them to proceed in the direction of redressing 96698-147
Income Tax Act
the balance between those who pay too little on too much and those who pay too much on too little.
Unfortunately the amendments which have been proposed do not clearly mark out that direction at all, much less strike out boldly in the direction of that social equality which should be the first objective of a democracy.

Mr. Speaker, on second reading of this bill I should like to say just a word. This Social Credit group, which has been in this house for quite a number of years, has not taken as much time in the house as generally is taken on a good many measures which some people may think deserve some attention, but which at times we have thought did not require all the attention which had been given to them. But when it comes to matters under the Department of Finance, whether it is taxation, inflation, tight money-no matter what the subject might be within the confines of that department-we feel that we have been sent here with a sort of special mission, a mission that will propose that which is right and proper in monetary fields and condemn those monetary policies which we believe work to the disadvantage of the people.
We are now considering Bill No. 232, which has been brought in by the Minister of Finance, and which he himself has declared is brought in more or less as a substitute for his budget. It deals with a reduction in the income tax. I might say we support the bill partly by compliment and partly by condemnation. The reduction proposed in this bill is commendable but puny. I think all will recognize that any reduction in income tax must be acceptable because it leaves that much more spending power in the hands of the consuming public, yet we do believe that there is a class of people which this reduction in income tax does not touch at all.
I refer to the particular class of people who are so poor they do not even reach the bracket of income where they must pay any income tax. It does not affect them at all, and they are the people who are more in need of consideration than any other class of people in the country. They are the old age pensioners who have to live on that which they receive by way of their pensions; they are the recipients of war veterans allowances, war veterans pensions, and all those social service benefits that go to them through the social service acts. People who may have to live on just those amounts of money are not affected by this bill. In other words, those who need it most cannot get any benefit from the present government's taxation policy.

Income Tax Act
There are other people who should be considered when legislation is proposed for a reduction of income tax. For a good many years many of us have been advocating the inclusion of medical expenses as a justifiable exemption in matters of income tax. This bill does not touch that matter at all, yet if any consideration is given it should be given to those who are burdened by expenses because of illness over which perhaps they have no control at all.
Just the other day I received a letter from a man who is a cripple. He cannot walk to work; he must have transportation. He cannot even get on a bus; he must be driven to his work in a car. He can drive a car although he is unable to walk. Well, the department will not allow him anything for the expense of operating his car. They will not allow any exemption for that. Yet we find that an employee or the manager of a company or firm is in a different position.
Perhaps he does not even own his own car and does not need to, because he is in a position where he can use a company car. The company gets an exemption for the running expenses of that car, but the poor man does not get any recognition with regard to the expenses of running his car, and if he happens to be a cripple a car is an absolute necessity.
It seems to me that is unjust. I think a good deal of our taxation legislation is unjust by reason of the principle of taxation, but it certainly is unjust when the poor and the needy are forgotten in matters of taxation policy.
Yesterday the hon. member for Port Arthur referred to the exemption of expenses of university students. I have brought up this matter at previous sessions. The university student works a little bit during the summer months to earn some money with which to go to university. During the time he is attending university his earning power is almost at a standstill. His father helps to finance him but the father gets no recognition for that except that the young man or young woman may be a dependant and the father gets the benefit of the $400 exemption allowance on income.
There are a lot of these cases that we could bring before the minister, but I am not going to labour this point. I do not want to get away from the actual principle of income tax. While the bill gives some relief to some taxpayers, it does not give relief to the very people who stand most in need of it.
In replying to certain discussion the other day the minister said that he was conscious

of the evils of taxation. He suggested that this is something nobody likes, but somehow or other the government feels that it must continue to tax. Of course I am not saying there should not be some form of reasonable taxation, but while the minister says that taxation is an evil but which he apparently regards as necessary, I find that the government will never countenance any suggestion that will lead to a reduction of taxation without affecting income. That is an important point.
As far as this group are concerned, we believe that taxation could be very considerably reduced if it were not for the fact that the government knows very well that when it spends money it must get the money from somewhere to spend. You cannot have it both ways, according to present government policy, which is the policy that was pursued by the previous government. As a matter of fact, so far as actual monetary policy is concerned there is no difference between the preceding administration and the present government. There is absolutely none. As a matter of fact, as far as I can see it does not take any particular brains to run a finance department if it is a matter of balancing income with expenditure.
In that case even you might make it.

In that case even I might make it, not that I want the job at all. The fact of the matter is that the finance minister is in an almost impossible position. He is trying to operate the finance department and determine financial policies under a financial system that does not work, that is not self-liquidating. Oh, I see Mr. Speaker rising.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have this opportunity of putting before the house a few observations which I arrived at as a result of discussions 96698-1474	1
Income Tax Act
with many of my constituents during the summer months concerning the tax changes which the people in my constituency thought they were going to get from the government in this first session of this parliament. I would preface my remarks by stating that the attitude which I and, I am sure, other C.C.F. members have taken with regard to the Income Tax Act is that it is part of a tax structure which is extremely unfair to the low income groups in Canada.
In my judgment the income tax was never intended as a tax to be levied against those on modest incomes. By its very nature the income tax was considered a means of taxing those on comfortable or high incomes. But over the years-and the war years gave an impetus to this downward movement-the exemptions under the income tax act in many countries have been pushed downward so that today there are many people in Canada who are required to pay income tax and who are earning salaries which place them at or near the subsistence level.
For example, we have minimum wage legislation in Canada. In my own province and in my own city that wage is $30 a week. I would suggest that the minimum wage is exactly what the name implies; it is the barest minimum on which a worker can be expected to live. Yet we have the strange situation that a single worker in Canada earning just over $20 a week-in other words $10 less than the minimum wage paid in the cities of Saskatchewan-is required to pay income tax. I suggest that the Income Tax Act in that respect is very unreasonable.
It is all very well to talk about inequities under the Income Tax Act, but I think over the years we in the C.C.F. group have suggested a means whereby we might remove from the income tax rolls at least a number of these people who are earning incomes so low that by no stretch of the imagination should they be considered to be earning enough to pay income tax. For many years we have advocated in this house that the exemption for income tax purposes for single taxpayers should be increased from $1,000 to $2,000 a year and for married taxpayers from $2,000 to $3,000.
I for one was highly elated last spring to find that the Conservative party, after many years, had finally arrived at the position where their policy was brought into line. Whether it was under the impetus of the election in the immediate future or for whatever reason, I do not know. Nevertheless they came out and suggested, declaimed, promised or pledged that if elected they would increase the exemption for single taxpayers from

Income Tax Act
$1,000 to $1,500, and that for married taxpayers the exemption would be raised from $2,000 to $3,000. Where the statement was made through the press or on the public platform, as was done by the Minister of Transport in his Gananoque speech, I can say one thing of the government, namely that the publicity work done on behalf of the Conservative party must have been very effective, because the people in my constituency were definitely under the impression that the government was going to increase the exemptions under the Income Tax Act as outlined just a moment ago. The promise was given, and I do not think any responsible Conservative can deny that that pledge was made in various ways and so effectively that people throughout Canada expected this type of reform in the Income Tax Act.
What has happened? There has been no move whatever to increase the exemptions. Thus we find the situation continuing where, as I say, single workers earning over $20 a week, which is below the minimum wage paid in those provinces of Canada which have minimum wage legislation, are yet required to pay income tax.
It is true that there has been a move to increase the exemption per child under the terms of the Income Tax Act. Here again at the present time a family with four children earning less than $2,600 a year is not affected by this move at all. In other words, as far as tax reductions are concerned that family is receiving no benefit whatsoever. I would remind the government that their promises with regard to tax reductions were not merely specific pledges to increase the exemptions, but there was a blanket assurance on the part of the Conservative government that they would cut taxes.
Last evening reference was made to their frequent claim that the pockets of the Canadian taxpayers were being picked to a certain extent. In my constituency I was often stopped in the street in the months of August and September by constituents who said, "When are you going down to Ottawa? When is parliament opening? When are we going to get those tax reductions?" The man in the street had been led to believe, as indeed the Prime Minister pledged, that his government would call a September session in order to cut taxes.
Hon. members supporting the government have made frequent boasts during the course of this session, and we shall probably hear a great many more, that they have kept their pledges, and that they have done all the things they promised to do. Here is one specific instance in which they are a far
IMr. Ellis.]
cry from the action which was promised by the government prior to June 10.
With respect to the vast number of Canadian citizens who, notwithstanding the great claims of prosperity in this country, are earning incomes so low that they are never called upon to pay income tax, there is no measure of tax relief whatsoever from this government. The old age pensioner on his mere pittance is still paying the sales tax on the necessities of life and in some instances excise tax on things which are necessary to life. There is no tax reduction for the pensioners, for those living on annuities, or who have retired on modest savings and who are not paying income tax because their income is not high enough. There is no measure of tax relief for that group of Canadian people.
I therefore suggest that when hon. members opposite get to their feet, pat themselves on the back and boast about how they have reduced taxes, they should explain why they consider that the vast number of Canadian people who are earning very low incomes should be ignored in this fashion. I should like the Minister of Finance to explain to the house why, in conformity with the pledges made by the government prior to the election, there is no provision to increase the exemptions for single or married taxpayers under the terms of this act, and to suggest to the house how the government can claim to have reduced taxes and to have kept their pledges with respect to tax reductions as long as they have failed to take any action to reduce the taxes paid by the people with the lowest incomes in this country. Such tax reduction can only be brought about through reductions in the sales tax, a tax which is levied on the lowest paid worker, the recipient of the lowest income in this country.
My colleague the hon. member for Van-couver-Kingsway suggested, with respect to the increase in the exemption, per child, that perhaps an even more effective way of granting assistance to family groups throughout this country would have been an increase in the family allowance. Such a move would certainly have extended benefits to all families in Canada, not merely to families which are earning incomes of over $2,600 a year. Whatever measure of tax relief is given, this legislation must be considered in terms of what the bill does not do and the vast number of Canadian people who are ignored under its terms.
I realize, Mr. Speaker, that when we talk about further tax reductions we are always asked, "Well, where is the government going to get this money? What is the alternative form of revenue?". I think the Minister of

Finance certainly has reason to expect suggestions as to how alternative forms of revenue can be obtained. I suggest however that, for one thing, the absence of a tax on capital gains is a pretty sad commentary on the tax structure in the country at the present time.
On former occasions members of this house have pointed out the part played by capital gains in the creation of large fortunes. As a matter of fact, if we were to go through the history of the large fortunes in Canada and the United States we would find that in the main the accumulation of that wealth was through capital gains and certainly not through salaries or wages, regardless of how large they might be. I think there might be some argument as to whether capital gains constitute income, but I believe the economists generally will agree that capital gains are income and, like other income, represent taxpaying ability.
That is the basis upon which taxes should be levied, on the ability of the individual to pay. Therefore the refusal of the government to face up to this problem and to tax Canadians on their ability to pay means that the greater part of the tax levied must be borne by the low-income groups who are living at the subsistance level. We find the incredible situation in Canada where Canadian workers, earning less than the minimum wage, are required to pay income tax.
As far as capital gains are concerned, the thing that must be borne in mind is that capital gains result from the sale of assets and that they are not too dissimilar from ordinary trading profits; but in any event the accumulation of wealth from capital gains represents on the part of the taxpayer the ability to pay, and that should be the basis upon which Canadians should be taxed.
There are a number of other matters with which I should certainly like to deal, but I would like to make some brief reference to the clause concerning the allowability of expenses to construction workers. This is something of course, in which I have been interested for some time. I come from a constituency-

Mr. Speaker, just to bring this overcrowded house up to date with regard to what I was saying prior to the noon recess, I was speaking of the special circumstances surrounding employment in the mining industry, where because of the nature of the industry many of the mines are located at high altitudes where for a number of reasons in some cases the members of the family are unable to reside with the employee. I have reference to several personal acquaintances of mine who are in just such circumstances. They are required to maintain their families in homes at a lower altitude and maintain themselves at the site of the operation. This circumstance works a great hardship on them. I feel that they should also be included in the provision that has been introduced in this amendment.
There are other circumstances surrounding employment in the mining industry to which we might also give some consideration. By the nature of its undertakings mining is a particular hazardous occupation. Miners are required by law to provide themselves with protective equipment such as hard hats and hard-toed shoes. In many instances a pair of leather boots which are accepted as the best footgear to meet safety requirements may cost up to $24 a pair, and the miner may
Income Tax Act
wear out two or three pairs of boots in one year. In some cases the mining company will pay a portion of the cost of this equipment by making deposits to the supplying retailer, but even when that has transpired a pair of leather shoes is said to last only six months at the most, and because of the acid content of the water to which they are exposed they deteriorate rapidly. The supplying of this equipment is a considerable expense for the miner, and this is another case where special consideration might be given.
The person who is employed on a wage or salary has no opportunity to make provision for any of these circumstances. In many instances a small businessman is given some latitude in determining what are actual expenses and what are not, and it may be that many of these small businesses are able to operate only because they are in a position to make these deductions from actual earnings. I think this is probably true in many cases, and there is still the basic difference between this group and those on salary that seems to discriminate against employees who work on a payroll basis.
For instance, an automobile is generally recognized as a necessity today. Business-men are able to make certain deductions which almost write off the cost of their automobiles, and in many instances they can deduct the cost of operating them. The cost of operating automobiles under normal circumstances would total approximately between $800 and $1,000 a year, and the value of the automobile is reduced by about $500 each year. We certainly cannot assume a cost of less than $1 a day for the maintenance of an automobile. This is an expense which must be met by those of us on wages and salaries who own cars, and we are given no consideration with respect to income tax deductions.
One hon. member mentioned earlier the question of the 2 per cent tax for old age security. I do not agree with the hon. member that this is irregular as he would seem to indicate, but I think there is room for some improvement here. The ceiling on old age security for income tax purposes could justifiably be increased. It would have the effect of bleeding off from those who are already in good financial circumstances and receiving the old age security pension a certain sum of money. It is generally understood they do not actually require the old age security payments, but for the purposes of administration everyone has been included in the act.
In addition to the parents of a university student I believe the student himself should be given special consideration in cases where he earns over $1,000 a year. He should be

Income Tax Act
exempt from taxation, because in view of the high cost of education $1,000 is not going to provide him with a full year of university training.
That is all I have to say on this question. I hope the minister will see fit to give consideration to these matters, and more particularly that he will include other categories of employees for exemption when living apart from their families.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, before my hon. friend is called on I wonder if hon. gentlemen would permit me to say this. Far be it from me to wish to ask any hon. member to curtail his remarks in any way. I am, however, one of the ministers who expect to leave to attend the NATO council meeting by plane at seven o'clock tonight. I cannot leave until this bill is disposed of, and I simply ask the consideration of hon. members under these rather cramping circumstances.
Short speeches, yes.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to assure the minister in my opening sentence that I intend to be very brief indeed. However, this is a field in which I have taken some particular interest over a number of years, and I would not like to see the opportunity pass by without expressing my pleasure at being able to endorse the principle of the bill we now have before us. I think its effect will be much more widespread than that of the bill we dealt with yesterday. I feel that in a much more direct manner the purchasing power of that section of the Canadian people whose purchasing power ought to be enhanced at this time especially is going to be aided by the passage of the bill that is now before us.
I am pleased to note that quite contrary to my expectations the new government we now have, that is now amending the Income Tax Act, is following what I feel is a sounder course than the old government followed when they gave tax relief under the Income Tax Act. What I have in mind here again relates to the urgent need to keep at a maximum the purchasing power of our Canadian people, because we are threatened with an apparent overproduction of consumer goods all along the line. When the old government made its last amendment to the Income Tax Act, as I recall it, the awards were made on a percentage basis, and the wealthy people who did not actually need a reduction in taxation were able to obtain benefit away in excess of what the ordinary taxpayer received.

One of the underlying principles of the amendment before us, as I see it, is that more or less all taxpayers in the country-and this applies to all corporations-are receiving an even sum of money which, of course, means that under this bill much more in proportion is to be given to the poor than to the rich. I feel that is something that is very desirable.
I should like to call the minister's attention to one thing with respect to the principle of the bill. I notice that he recognizes the need to raise the exemption for dependants. In my opinion the raising of the exemption for dependants is a much more urgent and pressing matter than reducing the rate of taxation. I do not think anyone can argue that we can bring up a child these days on the annual exemption allowed in the Income Tax Act. I have always failed to see the reasons for granting an adult an exemption of $1,000 and only a few hundred dollars for a dependant. If this government wishes to help family life in our nation they might well consider at some future time extending the principle they have adopted in this bill, namely the principle that the exemptions for dependent children should be raised. I rather regret that the sum allowed for a child is not at least $500.
I also wish to pass on a thought in connection with what the previous speaker and other speakers have already referred to, namely the principle that a certain class of workers who have to live away from home should be given an extra concession. I should like to impress upon the minister my belief at least that there are tens of thousands of other people, not necessarily all manual labourers, who must earn their living away from home, and I feel that to begin to discriminate as between one class and another of our Canadian citizens in the Income Tax Act is a regrettable thing. While I do not intend to oppose the adoption of the principle which the amendment signifies, I do feel that it has in it an element of discrimination.
I should also like to call the minister's attention to another problem, and I regret that it is not being touched here. About a year or so ago, when we had the last amendment to the Income Tax Act, there was a provision to encourage the Canadian people to save more money. We were granted the right to deduct the premiums paid on certain types of insurance and annuity policies. I notice no mention of that here, and I regret that. I hope the minister will look very carefully at the regulations which his department has drawn up under the existing Income Tax Act in that regard, because I feel the limitations which are being imposed are much too severe. I am sure the intent of the former minister

of finance is not being carried out by the very limiting restrictions which have been placed upon the types of insurance and annuity policies which are exempt.
The history of the Income Tax Act, Mr. Speaker, is that it was imposed during the first world war in order to help pay for the burden of that war. It was retained after the war, and the argument which has always been given for its retention rather than its abolition is that since a welfare program is under way in our Canadian life, the Income Tax Act is a useful instrument whereby the government might take from those who have more than enough in order to help, through various pieces of welfare legislation, those of our citizens who have less than enough.
At the present time we seem to have lost that intent of the Income Tax Act. While there is some recognition in the bill before us that the government seems to feel that we ought to return to the old intent of the Income Tax Act, and that they are prepared to grant some concessions, yet they have not changed the basic exemptions of the average worker. They remain at $1,000 for a single person and $2,000 for a married person. I realize the rates have been reduced, but the exemption has not been raised.
We have in our present economy a situation where we are levying an income tax on the below-average wage earner. I feel that this is putting a completely new purpose to the Income Tax Act, a purpose which I should like to see eliminated. I should like to see the day when exemptions are raised to the point where the average and below average wage earner are exempt from paying income tax.
Our proposal is that the exemptions should be raised to at least $1,500 for a single person and $3,000 for a man and his wife, with a dependant exemption of $500 for each child. I feel if that proposal were adopted the government would be going a long way toward making the Income Tax Act once again an income tax act and not a general measure of taxation of our people.

I shall not take the time of the house to repeat the arguments on some of the points that have been raised, but I should like to press the minister for a reply to the arguments advanced regarding the deductibility of medical expenses for income tax purposes. As the minister knows, on at least two occasions this session, as recorded on page 248 of Hansard for October 22 and on page 1896 of Hansard for December 5, I asked the minister whether the government would be doing something about this matter in line with the position taken by the Minister of Finance himself during the days when he was with us on this side of the house. As a matter of fact, the day before those proposals were announced I put my question to him and, of course, I was told to look back to a previous answer. I must not try to allege that the minister promised me he would make a statement, but I thought when he asked me to wait until that time I could look forward to some remarks on this question. It is now part of the law that a taxpayer can, without putting in any receipts, claim $100 blanket deductibility for medical expenses, charitable donations and trade union dues. Well, that

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is the first occasion, if my recollection serves me correctly, on which my hon. friend has invited me to make a speech. If my memory be faulty in that respect, it will certainly be the first occasion on which he has invited me to make a lengthy speech, when I fear I shall have to disappoint him.
There are many things I might, under ordinary circumstances, wish to say at this time, Mr. Speaker, but with the departure of the plane for Paris for this NATO meeting now only a matter of a few hours away I will ask the house to excuse me with only very brief comment on one or two points that have been raised.
Indeed, I think my comments should be of a general nature. Various suggestions have been put forward with regard to individual tax measures and tax reforms which are desirable in the view of those who have put them forward. Let me say in general that I came into this portfolio with an open mind on many of these questions, and also with the views I have already expressed on many of these questions in the past when a member of the opposition. I have not changed the views that were expressed then. I hope, given time and opportunity, to be able to carry further into effect some of the reforms that have been advocated by my colleagues and myself in times past.
But we cannot do it all in the first year. We cannot do it all in the first five months. We have gone as far as the limitations imposed upon us this year have permitted us to go. We simply had to accept the budget that was introduced last March on behalf of the previous government, and operate within

that budget. That is my general comment with regard to the various matters that have been mentioned here in the course of debate.
As to views that have been expressed by my colleagues or myself on specific matters in times past, we have gone, we think, under the existing circumstances and limitations, a long way at this time, and we hope the house will view the present proposals in that light, namely the light of the limitations that we inherited. Our efforts in this respect are not going to end now. We are going to go on seeking to do what we can in fulfilment of a program of tax reform.
My friend the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre asked me for a specific comment about the matter of the deduction of medical expenses. What I have just said applies to that matter. These and all other matters are going to receive continuing consideration. In my concluding remarks last Friday night I said something that evidently was taken up wrongly by those who followed me. I was trying to point out that the problems that have faced the government have been very heavy. We have done the best we could. We had a series of international conferences to prepare for and attend. We have done as much in this respect as I think flesh and blood can be expected to be equal to. We have not been able to do everything, but we are not going to stop our efforts now.
There are one or two matters that were touched upon that I think might more appropriately be dealt with in committee. I shall have a word to say there about this matter of the relief brought to construction workers, but I think those comments can more appropriately be made in the committee.

I would like to ask the minister just one question. I understood him to say that he was soon leaving for the NATO conference, and I do not think we want to hold things up; but would he care to state when he expects his estimates will be proceeded with? Will we wait until he returns, or what is the program?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The estimates of the Department of Finance cannot be called again in committee of supply until after we return from NATO, and the schedule calls for our being back, I think, just a matter of about three hours before the house adjourns for the Christmas recess.
Thank you.

On clause 1-Construction workers.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think I should offer the committee a brief statement on clause 1 in view of the fact that some hon. members in the debate on second reading raised questions about the extent of the tax relief provided by this clause.
As I indicated in an earlier statement, this clause is intended to provide a measure of relief for construction workers. I take it there is no issue as to the measure of tax relief afforded to construction workers, but questions were raised as to why they should be singled out for this particular consideration. Might I give the house a statement on that point, sir.
As I mentioned in my remarks last Friday night this is a new provision and, in its genesis, it goes back to a directive issued by the former government in the year 1956. Until that time there had been no attempt to include in the income of construction workers such allowances as are made to them by their employers for board and lodging when they were working away from home. That directive was confined to construction workers, and at no time in the consideration of this matter has any question been raised as to any other persons. The directive out of which the whole matter emanated related to construction workers and construction workers alone.
There was discussion of this matter in the house last spring, and at that time the former minister of finance said the new directive purported to treat from that point on, or gave notice that from that point on the government would treat such moneys as taxable income in the hands of construction workers. In the discussions in the house, and in face of protests from members of my party, the then minister of finance said the new directive would not be applied to income for the year 1956, but it would be applied as from January 1, 1957.
Shortly after coming into office we received representations on this point from both the construction industry and the Canadian Congress of Labour. These representations in every case have been confined to the construction worker. No representations have been made on behalf of any others.
I would not have the committee think this problem is free of difficulty. On the contrary, the whole matter is beset by some very serious administrative problems. We are, in a sense, opening a door and we will have to watch very closely the way this new provision works out, to see how the administrative problems are met. We are admittedly going a long way in this provision, but it
Income Tax Act
was indicated to us that some firms-for instance, those engaged in construction on the D.E.W. line-had found it difficult to persuade construction workers to go to that area in the face of the directive that had been issued and the statement of the former minister of finance that the directive would be applied to all allowances accruing after January 1, 1957.
A question was raised about loggers. We have received no representations on that score, and the Canadian Congress of Labour in its submissions to us on more than one occasion put the case on behalf of the construction worker, and the construction worker alone.
There is no union of loggers in our province; they appeal to their member for parliament.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
We have given to this plea of the construction workers very careful study and have brought forward this amendment, not without misgivings in regard to the difficulties of administration which might present themselves. I would, however, ask the committee to bear in mind that there has been no opportunity for giving consideration to the position of other workers who may consider that their tax position should be regarded as equivalent to that of the construction worker in the view embodied in the present clause.
Any attempt to deal with other groups would necessarily require the most careful study before any action could responsibly be taken. I am asking the committee therefore to approve the clause in this form, to give us an opportunity to watch-as we will watch very carefully-the application of the clause; and the matter will, I can assure the committee, be the subject of continuing study. I hope for that reason the committee will see fit to give us the opportunity to go forward with this clause, meeting as it does a problem, not of our creation, but a problem created by the directive of a year and a half ago; and will also give us the opportunity of seeing how this works out in operation and in administration before we are asked to revise it or to extend it.

I should like to direct a question to the minister. I wonder if he could tell us whether in a case where a worker whose talents and knowledge are essentially required and who is shifted about the country, say in the construction of aeroplanes, from his ordinary residence to the location where construction is going on, the term "construction worker" would also be applied

Income Tax Act
to that classification. Would the words "construction worker" also apply to this classification, because in reality they are construction workers. If a worker on the D.E.W. line is called a construction worker, then I think certainly an aeroplane construction worker might also be called a construction worker. Would the provisions of the bill also apply to those engineers who are summoned away from home for the purpose of helping in the construction of aeroplanes?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the hon. member is asking me for an advance interpretation of expressions used in this clause. I can only say to him that the interpretation will be a matter for the Department of National Revenue, and having regard to the purpose of the clause I am quite satisfied that the department will endeavour to place a fair and ample interpretation upon it.
As to what type of construction is contemplated here, the hon. member is seeking, I take it, to draw a distinction between someone who is engaged in constructing buildings which will become fixtures, part of the real estate, and someone who is engaged in constructing a chattel. I think I can say to him in this respect that a man who is engaged in the construction of a factory, a canal, a bridge or a road is obviously a construction worker. When it comes to the matter of fabricating an aeroplane or some chattel I should think that process would be more properly described as manufacturing than as constructing, for this purpose.

May I point out that I have a particular reason for asking this question. These are men of special talent whose ability and scientific knowledge are required. As a result of their particular knowledge and talent they are often summoned from one place to another. Would the minister not think these people should be placed in a special category, and that they should be offered the relief which the bill intends to provide?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am quite sure the hon. member is aware a man who is on, shall we call it, a travel status for his employer, a man who is travelling about on behalf of his employer, is not assessed for whatever the employer lays out as part of his travelling expenses or living allowance while engaged in his travels on behalf of his employer.

Mr. Chairman, I listened very carefully to the Minister of Finance when he spoke on clause 1 of the bill. I am sure the proposal which it contains in so far as construction workers are concerned will be welcomed. The minister made reference to a directive on which we had considerable

discussion in the house a year ago. As I understand it, the proposal for an amendment to the Income Tax Act which he is now bringing forward is in fact making legal something which, apparently, had been carried on as a practice in the industry over a number of years, a practice to which the Department of National Revenue has turned, more or less, a blind eye. I think that is obvious in the light of the directive we were discussing here last year under the name of bulletin No. 10.
Certainly I welcome the suggestion that discrimination against construction workers is to be eliminated. Nevertheless, from what the minister said in his opening statement it has become apparent that we will have to start all over again a wearing down process on the new Minister of Finance at a time when some of us felt we were beginning to penetrate the conscience of the former minister of finance to eliminate this kind of discrimination.
I must say that in listening to the Minister of Finance on the question of administrative problems I fail to follow his argument that because of administrative difficulties the broader provisions which some of us have been suggesting cannot be brought in at this time. Particular reference has been made to the situation of the loggers or bushworkers by a number of hon. members who have spoken earlier in this debate, and in pursuing the subject I should like to suggest that if the minister is thinking in terms of administrative problems he will really have a problem on his hands when he begins his attempt to determine whether or not certain workers are construction workers.
I would remind him that in some of the west coast logging camps where all the workers are organized in an industrial union there are probably a good many workers who are in construction classifications. The minister will find himself up against the peculiar difficulty of having to try to draw a fine dividing line between certain workers in these camps who can qualify as construction workers and certain others who, he will have the trouble of deciding, are not construction workers.
Earlier someone here was talking about a Pandora's box, and I think the minister, as a result of the approach he has made to this problem, has opened the way to a large number of administrative problems which he has not envisaged. The Minister of Finance has suggested that he has not had any representations on this matter of allowable deductions except on behalf of construction workers.
I quite agree with him that the Canadian Labour Congress has made a major point of

this question of construction workers, because it was a problem which had arisen as a result of this bulletin of the Department of National Revenue. But when he says he has not received any other representations at all, I do not know whether or not he is referring to the situation as far as the Department of Finance is concerned only since he took office. I do know, however, that I have in my hand a letter dated December 9 of this year addressed to him from what is known in British Columbia as the loggers' local of the international woodworkers of America.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: What is the date of the letter my hon. friend read?
December 9, 1957.

of the loggers in the entire logging industry *of British Columbia and Alberta. This is not a new problem at all nor one which has not had prior consideration within the Department of Finance.
I am going to turn for a few minutes to the debate which took place in this house last April when we were discussing the Income Tax Act. Following an extended discussion on the subject dealt with in clause 1 of this bill, as found at page 3035 of Hansard of April 3 last, I referred to statements that had been made by the then minister of finance and I said:

I agree in part with what the minister has been saying, namely that this problem is not something which is unique to the construction industry. As far as I am concerned, it applies equally, and as seriously, for example to the logging industry. In my opinion from the study I have made of the matter over the past several sessions, this whole question can be resolved only by a suitable amendment to the Income Tax Act-
Well, we now have an amendment to the Income Tax Act but the question as to whether it is a suitable one is open to debate. I went on to say:
-one that will remove what to me is a discrimination that now exists against the expenses that are incurred by those on wages and salaries in the course of earning a living.
As I said, I was refeiring at that time to some of the remarks that were made by the then minister of finance. I think I should point out that Mr. Harris made remarks which certainly should have come to the attention of the present minister if he has been giving any consideration to this problem. It will be found on page 3025 of Hansard of April 3, 1957, that Mr. Harris had this to say:
There is no question but that the construction industry is unusual in this field, yet it is not wholly

unique. There are other industries in which allowances for board and lodging are given.

We have been doing our best to find a rule which would tax every one with the same kind of income unless there was a real case to be made for an exception. I think all hon. members of the committee would agree with me on that score, namely that if there are exceptions-if I am being taxed for one thing that some hon. gentleman opposite is not being taxed for-there must be great justification for that exception to be made.
Later, on the same page, he went on to say:
We want to see that all other workers who are in about the same kind of situation will have their cases considered on their merits and we will be able to know where to draw the line with respect to the exemption, whether it should be drawn just at the construction workers or whether it should be extended beyond that.
On page 3028 he continued with remarks to the effect that he thought it was clear that he had no fixed idea on this matter but, however, he did want a consistent tax law.
Some of us were inclined at that time to say, "All right, let us have a little more patience about this question and be prepared to wait a little longer so that we can have a consistent tax law." I suggest that we have now waited for some months and while it is perfectly true that there has been a change of government and that we have a new Minister of Finance nevertheless I think it is apparent from those remarks made by the previous minister of finance that this is something which has not suddenly come under review within the Department of Finance and I can see no real reason why the present minister should not have been able to proceed to bring in a proposal that would have been equitable as far as all the working people of Canada are concerned.
It is interesting, of course, to discover that apparently our present Minister of Finance is able to put forward one point of view in one particular situation in one place and to put forward a rather different point of view when he is speaking to a different audience on some occasions. I have in my hand a copy of the Ottawa Citizen of December 10 and on page 3 there is a story which is headed, "Fleming Blasts U.S. Subsidiaries Lacking Canadian Shareholders". The story goes on at some length to describe the remarks made by the minister to the audience to which he was speaking on that occasion. Slightly changing the topic he suggested a few simple thoughts-
Well, I have heard it suggested on occasion-

What I am about to refer to is directly related to the topic under discussion, as I see it. The paper reports with respect to the Minister of Finance:

When the Minister of Finance was making that statement he was, in effect, agreeing with some of the statements made in this chamber last year by his predecessor when we were discussing the point that we have under consideration in this clause of Bill No. 232.
Earlier in my remarks I made reference to the fact that, having looked into the matter for several sessions, I had come to the conclusion that the problem with which we are dealing can be dealt with only by a suitable amendment to section 5 of the Income Tax Act. Well, we have before us in the committee today a proposal for an addition to section 5 of the Income Tax Act but, Mr. Chairman, in my opinion this is not a suitable amendment to the Income Tax Act because it is discriminatory and restrictive in its application. While, as I said earlier, it may be something that is welcomed by the construction workers at this time, nevertheless I am quite sure that they would be quite happy to see it applied to all other workers who find themselves in similar situations. Therefore, I should like to move:
That clause 1 be amended by deleting therefrom the word "construction" where it appears in lines 6, 12 and 13 on page 1, and in line 4 on page 2.
The clause as amended would then read:

Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) that this is too restrictive a clause.

In my opinion, the case of loggers and mine workers should have been particularly provided for.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to ask the minister several questions, one having to do with interpretation has already been brought up. In logging and especially in the pulp and paper industry there is a great deal of construction work involved and you cannot say that it is of a temporary nature because the whole course of the operation is towards permanency. If the company were to set up its bookkeeping operations in a suitable way, would it be possible to allow men detailed to that kind of work to have, instead of paying board and room, some adjustment of their wages to cover expenses

in order that they may qualify under the construction clause of the act? That is my first question.
Second, the minister seemed to suggest that no studies have been made in relation to woods workers. I would remind him of an answer that was given to me and which can be found on page 938 of Hansard. I asked the following questions:
Have any officials of the government made any studies and/or reports on the application and the possible effects of the extension of the expense deductions given to transport employees under subsection 7, section 11 of the Income Tax Act, to workers in either the woods or construction industry or both?
The answer was "yes". I realize that this is a slightly different section but I would infer from this that studies have been made with regard to woods workers. I should like to know the meaning of the statement the minister made in relation to that answer.
The third question I should like to ask has to do with the point the minister brought up about representation and strength of representation.
