I should like to ask the minister whether he feels that strength of representation is more important than just the straight fairness of the position.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, to the first question I would say at once that if the particular individual concerned is substantially engaged in construction he would certainly be regarded by the Department of National Revenue as a construction worker in the interpretation of this clause. I cannot think of a clearer case of a man who is a construction worker than someone who is engaged in road construction.
As to the second question and the written answer given in reply to my hon. friend's question as found at page 938 of Hansard, I draw his attention to the fact that his question was put this way:
Have any officials of the government made any studies and/or reports on the application and the possible effects of the extension of the expense deductions given to transport employees under subsection 7, section 11 of the Income Tax Act, to workers in either the woods or construction industry or both?
The answer was "yes". If my hon. friend expected a separate answer with regard to

each of these categories he should have put his question in proper form for that purpose. The answer is quite correct because a study had been made with regard to construction workers, as my hon. friend can see.
On his third point, it is not a matter of the strength of the representation in terms of the number of those for whom the spokesman speaks. That is not the simple basis upon which the decision ought to be taken. It is a question of the equities and the fairness of the case that is put forward. What are the intrinsic merits of the case? In my view every case ought to be considered on its merits regardless of the number of those affected. If there is injustice to one or two people then, if the proposed expedient is sound, that should call for the exercise of a legislative remedy if the merits of the case justify it.
But the point I was making earlier was that the representations we received, and there were many of them, were all on behalf of workers engaged in construction. We made a study of that subject and we felt there was a good case. We saw and can still see administrative difficulties involved. I hope that no hon. member thinks that we underestimate the administrative difficulties that may be involved. But we thought that there was a good case there on its intrinsic merits and that we should ask the house to deal with that case.
Since I became minister we have not received any representations on behalf of other groups. What I tried to convey in my opening remarks on this clause was that every case would have to be considered and studied very carefully on its merits. Certainly I would not be in a position today to say that any other particular group should have similar legislative consideration extended to it.
We are prepared to look at any such case and assess it on its intrinsic merits. But here today, in the absence of such thorough-going study, I do not think my hon. friend would expect a snap decision or a commitment to be given by the Minister of Finance.

Further to the answers that were given, may I say this. I have no desire to score on the minister and I am sure he has no desire to score on me in reference to the answer I read in Hansard. But it just points up the fact that the "yes" which I thought was all embracing only partially covered the question. I will see that in future my questions are more specific. But on the point of definition may I ask this question. If, as I plan to do as a result of the minister's remarks, I write to the pulp and paper companies in the region in which I am interested and inform them of the gist of the minister's statement
Income Tax Act
and advise them to set up matters so that when people are on specific construction jobs the evidence of that fact will be very clear, would the minister see anything out of order in that or anything out of principle?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It will be a matter to be decided in each individual case as to whether the particular taxpayer is a construction worker within the meaning of the clause; and that will be a matter of proof by evidence.

There are a number of questions I should like to ask arising out of the minister's statement that the details would be left to the department officials to interpret. In view of the discussion we had in the house in the early part of April with regard to this matter, there are several things that I should like to clear up. The minister will recall that a great deal of the argument revolved around the question of whether a construction worker was a permanent employee or a temporary employee, and the former minister of finance argued that if a construction worker was not employed on a year round basis he would under no circumstances be able to claim exemption. I should like to ask the present minister whether any distinction is being made under this amendment as between temporary employees and permanent employees. In other words, if a construction worker takes a job with a firm which lasts through the winter months, just because that firm is not in a position to guarantee that he will be carried on the payroll throughout the following summer or the following winter, is this construction worker on that account going to be denied exemption under the present amendment?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think the answer to my hon. friend's question was given by me earlier in reply to an earlier question. Let us take the case of the permanent employee. The case was given earlier of an engineer who goes about on behalf of a construction firm engaged in overseeing construction projects. If that man is a permanent employee and is travelling on behalf of his employer I think you will find that in every case his travelling expenses are covered by his employer. There is no problem with regard to him. But let us take the case of that firm or that engineer hiring persons to go out on a particular job, we will say for a month, two months, three months or four months. That latter is the man on whose behalf this particular clause is introduced. As long as he receives that allowance for board and lodging within the terms of this clause, in his capacity as a construction worker, from his employer he will, in respect of that allowance so received by him, now receive exemption under this clause.

Income Tax Act

The other question has to do
again with an interpretation placed on this matter by the former minister of finance and which seemed to indicate that if a group of employees, in a desire to maintain employment for themselves during the winter months, were required to leave their normal place of residence in order to get work they would not be considered as employees entitled to exemption by virtue of the fact that they were not employed by a particular firm and were not travelling to the new place of employment on the orders of the company. My question is this. If during the winter months a group of carpenters find that there is no work in their own locality and if on their own, in order to maintain employment, in order to maintain their household in their normal place of residence, leave their home to take employment elsewhere, will they be entitled to the exemptions under this bill before us?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think it is clear from the clause that the worker in question, if he leaves home on his own in search of employment is in this position. We will say he goes from Ottawa to Aylmer in search of employment in the construction industry. The expense incurred by him in that respect does not come within the terms of this clause. But if, on obtaining employment in Aylmer, the nature of his employment is such as to bring him within the terms of the clause, then he will receive the benefit of the clause. In other words, every case has to be dealt with on its own facts. But if I correctly apprehend the example given by my hon. friend, namely, the man who goes away from home in search of work, if there is no more than that to the case it is not covered.

The reason I asked the question is this. There are a number of workers in my own constituency who find work slack during the winter months. They are tradesmen. If they find that they can get employment in some other locality they leave. They cannot move their families; they cannot uproot their families and move to a new community on a temporary basis. Knowing that there is employment, or having good reason to believe that they can get employment in some neighbouring community, they leave and get work for a number of months. The thing I am concerned about is this. Just because they do not work for a particular construction company and travel to the new job on the orders or as employees of that company, I do not think they should be denied this exemption. I still feel that the workers in question should be entitled to deduct their expenses just as would the employees who work for a particular company and who move on instructions of the employer.

I have tried to make my point quite clear. As I say, it stems from the rather categorical statement made last year when we discussed this matter in the house by the then minister of finance, who argued point blank that if these people went on their own, unless they were ordered to do so by their employers they were not entitled to any consideration.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend will recall that this clause applies to allowances in respect of board and lodging or something equivalent paid by the employer to the employee. Obviously, in the case cited by my hon. friend the individual concerned is not receiving payment from the employer.

That is the very point I was trying to lead up, namely the manner in which this amendment is limited. It is not a question of giving consideration to construction workers who must leave their normal place of residence. There are laid down in the amendment conditions which will deny to many construction and other workers who must leave their homes in order to provide their families with a pay cheque any benefit under the section which we are now considering. That was my point in bringing this matter to the attention of the minister. I feel that the section is not broad enough. Notwithstanding the worthy objectives outlined by the minister, there are still in my own constituency many who are not going to obtain any benefit at all under the provisions of this bill, even though, in order to provide for the needs of their families, they find it necessary to leave their normal place of residence.
Shall clause 1 carry?

I should like to put one more question to the minister. Let us take the case of a group of, we will say, woodsmen, working for a pulp and paper company and engaged in the operation of cutting down pulpwood and so on. Suppose the pulp and paper mill decide they want to build a road and take a group of these men from the logging operation and put them at constructing a road. They clear a right of way for the road and probably work on it for one, two, three or four months or even a year or so on that kind of work. Where would it put them if they were allowed benefits for that time and then when they went back to their old jobs.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think in a case like that, the Department of National Revenue would have to examine the question very closely to see whether in essence, having regard to all the circumstances, the man is substantially a construction worker.

I would like to raise one question on subsection (b) of clause 1. I note there it says:
The value of, or an allowance (not in excess of a reasonable amount)-
My question is, firstly, who decides the mode of transportation; is it the employee or the employer. Secondly, what is considered a reasonable amount? For example, how is it determined whether one should travel by air, by car or by bus and so on?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not think I can lay down any hard and fast categorical rule as to the particular mode of transportation to be used. I suppose, if in any case a dispute arose as to whether an allowance had been extravagant, it would be necessary for the department to examine the allowance made for transportation as compared with the cost of transportation available to the worker in the circumstances and if it were to appear that the amount was in excess of what was the fare required in any acceptable and normal form of transportation then a question might be raised about it.
However, I think it is most unlikely that any serious problem will arise in determining a reasonable allowance for that purpose. If a man were, we will say, to hire a motor car or to use his own car and charge up at the rate of 50 cents a mile instead of the normal and usual charge made by employees of say nine or ten cents a mile, then that would be regarded as unreasonable and as an obvious attempt to pad. It is a question to be determined in every case in the light of all the circumstances.

What I had in mind was whether the employee or the employer decides the method of transportation. For instance, if an employer says a man should be transferred from a job in the Kitimat area to one at Stewart for example, which is just a straight case of using such methods of transportation as are available-it might be transport by boat from one place to another and if the time element entered the picture it might be air-will the decision depend upon the method determined by the employer or will it be the one the employee chooses to take in the circumstances?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
This is not a new type of legislation, Mr. Chairman. The Department of National Revenue is dealing with these cases with respect to transportation allowances all the time and there will be no more difficulty in interpreting and applying this clause than there has been in the thousands of cases with which the department is now dealing.
Income Tax Act

Mr. Chairman, I would like to direct a question to the minister in clarification of a point raised by the hon. member for Regina City with respect to this matter of travelling expenses. As I read the clause, on the question of travelling expenses one has to refer to subclause (a) (i) which says in part:
-in the course or by virtue of his employment as a construction worker-
Now I think a question does arise there in view of what the minister has said about not going along with the suggestion made by the hon. member for Regina City as to what is going to be the interpretation of the point at which employment commences.
I would phrase my question in this way: If a construction worker is referred by the officers of the national employment service to do a job and the situation is such that there is no local hiring agency or office of the construction company at the place from which he leaves and the formalities with respect to his employment are not completed until he actually arrives at this job, in that case may it not be considered that by virtue of his employment he would be entitled to his travelling expenses in going to the job.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not unless the employer provided an allowance for the worker in those circumstances as a term of his employment.

Well does the minister mean to say that if it is not the practice of a particular employer-as is sometimes the case in the logging industry-to advance fares before a man leaves his home and that man has to pay his own way to the job and is not reimbursed by the company, he will not be entitled to this exemption?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My friend's question takes us into an entirely new field, entirely new and quite outside the scope of the present clause. He is raising the whole auestion of the definition of expenses under section 11 of the act, expenses laid out for the purpose of earning income. Now that does not arise under this clause at all; this is a clause dealing with allowances by an employer to an employee and my friend's question does not arise here at all. It takes us into the interpretation of an entirely different section of the act.
I might say that section 11 was put in the act a long time ago and has been the subject of constant interpretation. It is a matter of determination in every case under section 11, whether an expense is incurred or an expenditure is laid out for the purpose of earning the income. If a man goes to another place to look for work, I think the department in that case is not going to treat his expenses as being laid out for the purpose

Income Tax Act
of earning the income. However, I must take the position that this question does not arise under this clause at all. We are entering a different field, a different part of the act entirely.

Mr. Chairman, on this point, the provisions under section 11 of the act, as I have always been led to believe in the discussions raised on this point, are provisions for expense allowances which are allowed to certain categories of people, such as travelling salesmen etc. Those on wages and salaries have been specifically denied these provisions under section 11 of the act because of the provisions of section 5 and my understanding is that the only way in which those in receipt of income from wages and salaries can qualify for any of these deductions enjoyed by other people is, as I suggested earlier, for a suitable amendment to be made to section 5 of the act which is a limiting section. As I understand it, those whose incomes come from wages and salaries can only deduct expenses for certain specific things. Now I fail to see that the question I have raised is not relevant to the proposal that the minister is bringing forward to provide an exemption for certain additional expenses under section 5 of the act.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the opening words of section 5 state:
Income for a taxation year from an office or employment is the salary, wages and other remuneration, including gratuities, received by the taxpayer in the year plus
(a) the value of board, lodging and other benefits-
Of any kind whatsoever, and so on. The purpose of the amendment is to provide that in the cases defined by the clause now under debate the construction worker does not carry that allowance from the employer into his income upon which tax may be levied.

May I suggest to the Minister of Finance that the coal miners cannot carry that expenditure into their income tax either. Why should it be that just one certain branch of industry is allowed this exemption? Why should not other workers be entitled to the benefit of its provisions? In the mining industry it often happens that the owner of a mine will transfer some of his help to another mine under his ownership, yet the men concerned are not allowed to make this deduction. A particular case occurs to me where men employed in a mine in Evansburg were moved to Drum-heller, still employed by the same company. I think this is a case quite parallel to the conditions under which construction workers are employed. Thus we find that one group of workers are penalized because they do not

receive the concession granted to another group. It seems hardly fair that while we are giving this assistance to one group of people, another group should not be receiving it. I think this provision should be made sufficiently broad to cover all industries where a similar situation exists.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I gather that the hon. member was not in the committee earlier this afternoon when we were reviewing this subject. There was an extended discussion of this point.

As hon. members of the committee realize, when earlier today I proposed an amendment which would have met the point so laudably raised by the hon. member for Bow River, you, Mr. Chairman, ruled that the amendment was out of order. The question of order was mentioned by my colleague the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. Your Honour may have realized that it was partly because of the impending departure of the Minister of Finance that he did not deal with this point of order more extensively than he did, and I should like to say this: in view of all the discussion which has taken place on this question, and in view of suggestions which he made, and to which I myself referred earlier, that amendments to the tax laws should be non-discriminatory in their application, the minister could leave for Paris with a much clearer conscience and expect to have a much happier reception on his return to Canada if he would consider accepting the amendment which I proposed, and moving it himself before he leaves on this important mission.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I assure the hon. member that if we do not get on with this section I will not be getting to Paris anyway.

Mr. Chairman, on clause 2, I think the increase in the allowable exemptions to dependents was a good move by the minister when he introduced his baby budget, but I do feel that it falls far short of the campaign promises which were made by the Conservative party. It seems to me that to implement their campaign promises would require a much larger exemption on account of dependent children, and for that reason we in this group are proposing at this time that the $250 exemption be increased to $500 for a child of family allowance age, and that the exemption of $500 should be increased to $750 for a child beyond family allowance age.

During the recent election campaign the Conservative party made much of its statement that the previous government had overtaxed the people by $500 million. Time and time again throughout the campaign the Prime Minister made the statement that the average family was being overtaxed by $120 a year, or $10 a month. He put this statement in another way when he said that every Canadian man, woman and child had had their pockets picked by $30. The proposal I am about to make would, if followed, result in the government meeting and carrying out its own campaign statements to the effect that the average family is overtaxed by $120.
I have here an example of an income tax payer who has an income of $4,000, and who has two dependants of family allowance age. Under the Harris budget, with a taxable income of $1,700, this taxpayer would pay $235 in the course of a full year. Under the proposal I am suggesting, increasing the allowance to $500, this taxpayer would pay $110, representing a saving of $125. This, as I say, is in line with the Prime Minister's statement during the election campaign and it goes a good deal beyond the tax relief granted by the Minister of Finance in his budget.
There is an overlying reason why I have advocated such an increase. I feel that the previous government made a very drastic mistake when they did nothing over many years to prevent family allowances losing their purchasing power, and I have calculated that to restore family allowances to the purchasing power they had when they first became effective in 1945 will take an increase of 64 per cent on the basis of the amount set at that time. Proposals for an increase along these lines were not accepted by the previous government and they are not being accepted by this government, and I feel the suggestion I am now making is a realistic alternative to the suggestion that we in this group have made for so many years that family allowances should be increased by 60 per cent over the 1945 rate in order to restore their purchasing power.
Because of this argument-the desirability of giving the income tax earner something which would provide him with some real measure of relief-I move:
That clause 2 be amended by deleting the figure "$250" from lines 19, 25 and 32, and by substituting therefor the figure "$500", and also by deleting the figure "$500" from lines 20, 26 and 32 and by substituting therefor the figure "$750".
The government said during the election campaign that the public of this country had been overtaxed by $500 million and yet the Minister of Finance in his budget-his peanut budget-said that the total tax relief would
Income Tax Act
amount to $146 million. If you add to that the amount the government is increasing expenditures from the national treasury in other fields you still arrive at a total that is far short of the $500 million tax relief that was so clearly a commitment made by the present government in the election campaign to the people of Canada. The motion I have moved on behalf of this group is certainly in line with the promises of the Conservative party and is directed toward seeing that the government fulfils its own election promises.

I submit to Your Honour that this wrenches any ruling that was made yesterday completely out of all recognition and I would ask Your Honour to rule the amendment out of order.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, despite the fact that I seem to have collected something of the voice of the hon. member for Coast-Capilano, I would be prepared if necessary to argue this point of order at length. I am satisfied, however, that it is not necessary to do so. In fact, I wondered when the Minister of Public Works got up where he was yesterday.
This amendment is on all fours with the amendment that was moved yesterday. Yesterday it was an amendment in committee to a taxation bill which had not been preceded by a ways and means resolution and it was an amendment that proposed a further reduction in a tax which the government was asking parliament to reduce. Today we have exactly the same thing. Today we have a taxation bill which was not preceded by a ways and means resolution in which the government is asking for a reduction in a certain tax. This amendment seeks a further reduction in that same tax.
The Minister of Public Works seems to have added some new words to his vocabulary since he moved across the way. He now says this would be a farce. May I say, Mr. Chairman, that if there is any farce so far as the proceedings in connection with this budget are concerned they relate to the failure of the government to precede taxation

Income Tax Act
measures with proper ways and means resolutions. I would like to take this opportunity, sir, of congratulating you on making a ruling at eight o'clock yesterday which was consistent with the ruling which Mr. Speaker made last Monday. I think everyone knows that I did not agree with the ruling which Mr. Speaker made on Monday but once he made it I accepted it and, having accepted it, my whole argument yesterday was that you, sir, should make a ruling consistent with the position that the Speaker took when he was in the chair and I do not think it is inappropriate for me to congratulate you on the ruling that you made and on its absolute consistency.
The Minister of Public Works said that if Your Honour did accept this amendment it would make a farce out of our financial proceedings. I say if there is any farce it is the government's own fault. I say to the Minister of Public Works, one who belongs to the Conservative party which a year ago wanted the rule of law to be preserved in this house, that he is asking Your Honour to make a farce out of procedure. He is urging you to make a ruling directly opposite to the ruling you made after due consideration at eight o'clock last evening. As I say, if hon. members on the government benches want to proceed with a procedural debate they can have it but relying on the consistency of the ruling that Your Honour made last night I do not think it is necessary.
Your Honour recognizes that I did not press the point with regard to the amendment that my colleague the hon. member for Comox-Alberni made to clause 1 of this bill. I must say I think Your Honour had a point in suggesting that perhaps there was something slightly irrelevant to what was before the committee in clause 1 but there is no irrelevance so far as this amendment to clause 2 is concerned. This amendment seeks to do exactly what was sought to be done by the amendment proposed yesterday, namely to ask for a reduction in a tax further to the reduction proposed by the government. All the citations we cited from May and the other authorities and the excellent citations you read from Campion all support the validity of the position you took yesterday, a position which I feel you have no alternative but to take again today.
I can see that the advantage of the ruling yesterday and the advantage of what is now happening may be that the government will not again make the mistake it made at this session in bringing in a budget without following the proper budget procedure but that is of their own making, even against our advice. In view of the present situation and

in view of the ruling you made last night I trust you will make a proper and consistent ruling at this time and accept the amendment that has been moved on our behalf by my friend the hon. member for Assiniboia.

In looking at this amendment I still feel that this amendment seeks a reduction in taxes and therefore I will have to rule that it is in order.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is a bill which I have had the privilege of presenting to the house on previous occasions. I hope that it may fare better in this parliament than it has in the past. As a matter of fact, I have had the privilege of presenting from time to time two bills which are companions to each other, one calling for annual holidays with pay, and this one calling for statutory holidays with pay.
It was something of a satisfaction when the speech from the throne was read at the opening of this parliament to discover that the new government had taken notice of at least one of these matters and promised that provision would be made for a bill to provide annual holidays with pay. That, of course, is another matter, and one which is under debate under two other orders but, as I say, it is good to note that by bringing these matters before parliament from time to time some progress is made.
I confess that just now when I looked at the speech from the throne to find the reference to the labour legislation that was to be introduced I happened to glance at another paragraph in that speech. I am afraid I would be out of order if I read it now, but it is my view that this particular paragraph-the second paragraph in the speech from the throne-has been blacked out by what happened here a little while ago.

subtopic: PROVISION OF STATUTORY HOLIDAYS WITH PAY FOR EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
Who
is calling order?
Mr. Speaker, it is readily recognized in this day and age that the time has come for

workers in industry to have as a matter of right certain time off, not only annual vacations with pay but statutory holidays. Progress in this field in Canada has been very slow to date. As far as I can ascertain, only six provinces have any legislation regarding statutory holidays. Those six are Newfoundland, Nova Scotia, Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia- two in the east and the four in the west. Even the legislation which these provinces have is in most instances not very advanced. In the case of Newfoundland and British Columbia, according to the latest information I have been able to obtain, all the legislation does is to state that certain days are public holidays. No provision is made in the legislation of these two provinces for overtime rates of pay for those who work on those holidays, or for pay as a matter of right on those holidays to those who are let off from their regular work.
In the other four provinces, Nova Scotia, Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, the legislation goes one step further inasmuch as provision is made for certain statutory holidays and for those who work on them to be paid at rates set out either in legislation or in regulations made under the legislation. These rates of pay vary. In most cases the legislation provides for overtime rates to a varying extent.
In only one of the six provinces I have just named does the legislation go all the way. That one province is Saskatchewan, where in the matter of statutory holidays there is, first of all, provision for such holidays to be observed; where there is, in the second place, provision for an overtime rate of pay for those who are required to work on statutory holidays; and in the third place provision that all employees who are entitled to these holidays get paid for them at their regular rate of pay, without having to work on those days.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this legislation is to introduce that principle at the federal level. Everyone knows that labour legislation in this country is the subject of divided jurisdiction, that most of our workers come under provincial jurisdiction, leaving about 10 per cent of our workers under federal labour jurisdiction. Because of this situation it has been a matter of interest to those of us who follow these things that the federal authorities should take the lead so that this legislation should not only bring benefit to those workers who are under federal labour jurisdiction but in order that the provinces may be encouraged to follow suit.

In this instance, therefore, we are asking the federal government not just to do something which the provinces have done, because the provinces have not gone very far in this field; we are asking that the federal government should take the lead. Let it be perfectly clear that any law with regard to labour which the federal government may pass does not impose any legal obligation on the provinces. But it does have a moral effect in that the provinces feel that they have to pay some attention to it. It is on that basis that we are pressing this legislation now and placing it before the House of Commons.
Those who argue against this legislation- and I know what the arguments are because we have had this bill up before-contend sometimes that the federal government should not get too far ahead of the provinces. To me that argument seems so weak that it hardly calls for an answer although I have already answered it. Another argument used by those who would oppose this kind of legislation is that this is a matter to be left to collective bargaining. That is an argument we have had to meet all along the line as far as labour legislation is concerned. Everything, from hours of work, the number of days to be worked a week, wages, working conditions, everything on which labour has sought legislation has been met with the argument that this should be left to bargaining between employers and employees. In the early days it was not even collective bargaining, it was just a matter of leaving it to employers and employees, and in practical terms that meant leaving it to the employers.
Today we have reached the stage of collective bargaining and the tendency of those who are opposed to this kind of legislation is still to suggest that this should be left to machinery of this kind. We have had to face that argument in the House of Commons with regard to such matters as annual vacations with pay, yet this session there is not only my bill but a government bill on the order paper dealing with this matter. We have had to meet this same argument with regard to equal pay for equal work; we have had to meet it with regard to fair employment practices; we had to meet it a number of years ago with regard to the protection of pension rights. I remember raising this matter, seemingly times without number, and being told by the late Humphrey Mitchell and others that this was not a matter concerning which we should seek to enact legislation. But, ultimately, the house did enact legislation protecting pension rights against loss due to strikes or lockouts, along the lines I had proposed.
And so, step by step, it has been recognized that there are certain rules of the game, certain labour practices, which in all fairness
Industrial Relations
should be regulated by legislation. There is no doubt in my mind but that sooner or later this one will be recognized as other matters have been so recognized. My plea is that it be sooner rather than later and so I present this bill to the house. As I say, it is the same bill that has been presented on previous occasions. It proposes that all the workers who come under federal labour jurisdiction shall be given certain holidays off work with full pay, those holidays being New Year's day, Good Friday, Victoria day, July 1, Labour day, Thanksgiving day, Remembrance day and Christmas day.
I might point out that these are the holidays that are observed for the most part in all parts of this country. There are some holidays that are observed only in certain areas such as the civic holiday that we observe in some areas on the first Monday in August and then there are holidays like St. Jean Baptiste day that are observed in the province of Quebec. My bill provides for a minimum of eight statutory holidays a year with pay leaving it to the possibility of provincial legislation extending it to some of those holidays that are observed locally if this is desired.
May I point out that my bill of necessity is one containing quite a few details. That is what devolves upon one when he presents a bill rather than a resolution. In a resolution one can ask for consideration of a general proposition and not have to take the responsibility of spelling out the details but these resolutions that state general propositions seem to take much longer to reach the statute books than an actual bill. It is also true that by means of a bill one can get debate in this hour from five to six that cannot be had in the case of resolutions. Nevertheless, Mr. Speaker, I urge upon hon. members to realize that when we are dealing with the second reading of a bill we are dealing with its principle.
Now, if there are some details of the bill that some hon. members think go a little too far, or not far enough, or which they think should be changed, let it be clear that those changes could be considered and effected in the industrial relations committee to which, after second reading, I would move that this bill be referred. For example, I am sure there will be differences of opinion in this house as to the rate of overtime pay to be provided for those who are required to work on statutory holidays so as to keep essential services in operation. The rate I suggest is in the bill. At this moment I refrain even from mentioning it although I suppose I should not because it is a detail in one of the clauses but my main reason for refraining from mentioning it is to urge that hon. members not

Industrial Relations
oppose the bill because they consider that this particular rate is too high or too low. That is one of the details that could be considered, discussed and amended if necessary in the committee. What is before us at this time on second reading is not the details of the bill but the broad general principle and that broad general principle is one that the Canadian Labour Congress has placed before the government in its submissions in October. It is a principle which I believe commends itself generally to members of this house and I hope the house will approve it. That principle is a very simple one, that the workers of this country who come under federal labour jurisdiction should be granted by legislation of this parliament at least eight statutory holidays a year with pay. I urge the house to adopt this bill.

subtopic: PROVISION OF STATUTORY HOLIDAYS WITH PAY FOR EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not think there will be much disagreement with the principle of this bill as outlined by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre with regard to the granting of eight statutory holidays a year with pay to those who come under federal labour jurisdiction. It has been admitted by the hon. member who introduced the bill that there is a certain conflict of jurisdiction, perhaps an overlapping, between the governments of the provinces and the federal government but I think if one surveys the pertinent legislation on the statute books of the provinces from coast to coast one will find that the bill proposed by the hon. member does not interfere to any significant degree with the broad general principle laid down in this bill that there be at least eight statutory holidays in the year.
My personal feeling is that the suggested holidays are not spaced as well as they could be. In fact, I would go much further than the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) who suggested eight statutory holidays and I would propose that we endeavour to arrange to have one statutory holiday occur in each month of the year.
At the present time we have one in January and then there is a hiatus until we come to Good Friday. Then we have Victoria day and Dominion day. Many municipalities hold a civic holiday on the first Monday in August. After that we have Labour day followed by Thanksgiving day. We have made a provision for Remembrance day to be observed as a statutory holiday although it is very seldom observed. Finally, in the last month of the year, we have Christmas day.
Perhaps it could be arranged to have a statutory holiday occur in February and St. Valentine's day would probably be acceptable to everyone as a suggestion. We could also

arrange to have one in March and probably my good friend who sits smiling on the other side of the house would agree that there is a certain day in March that would be highly acceptable to Irishmen. I am thinking, of course, of St. Patrick's day the patron saint of the Irish. This would serve to place a holiday in each month with the exception of June and I do not think there would be much difficulty involved in selecting a suitable holiday in that month.

speechtext: The 10th.

subtopic: PROVISION OF STATUTORY HOLIDAYS WITH PAY FOR EMPLOYEES
speechtext: The 24th, St. Jean Baptiste day.

subtopic: PROVISION OF STATUTORY HOLIDAYS WITH PAY FOR EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
Yes, probably everyone would be agreeable to accepting St. Jean Baptiste day and surely no one could disagree if we were to find a day in July to honour the other group of Irishmen, the Orangemen, and transfer the holiday from July 1 to July 12 in order that they might be included in the picture. The civic holiday in August to which I have already referred would serve to round out the picture as far as observing a holiday in every month of the year is concerned. I think both labour and management would be satisfied to accept the principle I have outlined.
In my working days there never was any difficulty in securing these holidays off from work. We were always given these holidays whether or not we had a union but although it was recognized that we would have these statutory holidays we experienced difficulty in getting paid for them. When it was decided that we should be paid for them the question arose as to what basis of pay we would receive. In the first instance we received normal pay, then time and a quarter, then time and a half, and finally double time. At present if a statutory holiday occurs while you are enjoying a regular vacation with pay and you are required to work on that day you receive normal pay plus double time and in effect you receive three days' pay for one day's work. Some workers regardless of how genuine their identification with the union is are quite eager to work on a holiday in those circumstances where they can receive three days' pay for one day's work. That is the picture of statutory holidays in this country in the future as I see it. If we work toward that end I think we will attain it.
There is also the problem that we found during the war. There was a considerable abuse of statutory holidays. The problem was this. When you gave a statutory holiday and they are paid for it they want to take the following day off to finish up the celebration, or probably the day before. Then a rule was brought in at the suggestion of

the union in an attempt to defeat absenteeism or prevent it. A rule was laid down that the employee would have to be at work the day before and the day after. There was not too much difficulty about it. When they got paid for the holiday I suppose they thought they could take one for themselves. When the war was on, absenteeism of that kind cut down production, and it was made part and parcel of the union agreement, and I think rightly so. Anyone who has had any dealings with the unions, as I have had for a good many years, knows that there has to be production in order to pay the wages. If we have a five-day week and a statutory holiday comes within that week, that reduces the week to four days, and if you have an employee who takes a holiday on his own, that cuts his week's work down to three days. That is all the work you will get out of him in that week. I think my good friend from Winnipeg North Centre would agree with me on that.
Paragraph (b) of section 2 reads:
"full time employee" means any employee who, in a week in which a statutory holiday occurs, works or is required to be at the disposal of his employer not less than 28 hours exclusive of overtime and any time the employee works or is required to be at the disposal of the employer on that holiday.
This paragraph can be interpreted in this way. The 28 hours that he has to work in a week could be four 7-hour days in that week, or it could be three 8-hour days and a half. If the latter were applied to statutory holidays it would defeat the purpose that the union had in mind that a man must work the day before or the day after. There is not too much trouble with that particular phase of it because most of the holidays are now arranged so that they come on Monday in order to give the employees a longer weekend. There is no difficulty with the day before the holiday. It is the day after that causes the difficulty. There has been quite a shemozzle over that one. If the employee does not turn up the day after he still thinks he should be paid for the holiday regardless of union agreement. An equitable arrangement was worked out whereby employees would be paid for the statutory holiday if they appeared the day after. In other words, if they appeared at nine or ten o'clock in the morning the day following, they would receive the same for the holiday. That was a compromise.
These are the difficulties that are encountered in ordinary industry, but probably they would not apply so much here with union employees because they are more or less on a contract basis and would turn up to work the next day. Nevertheless, industry as a
Industrial Relations
whole has probably solved this. It is not what you might call a pressing problem with labour now because it is generally recognized by employers that employees get these statutory holidays and the other holidays such as Christmas day or New Year's day and probably July 1, which is Dominion day, would be problem ones. Those are movable holidays; they may come at the beginning, in the middle or at the end of the week. Holidays such as Good Friday create no difficulty whatever. Labour day is a holiday which comes on Monday and so does Thanksgiving day. The civic holiday in August is generally on a Monday. Therefore, what is involved here is the day after. There is no difficulty here. This bill is to take care of federal employees.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has advanced his arguments and is bringing this matter to the attention of those who work for the federal government. There are some difficulties involved in the arrangements for the taking of those holidays, and I have mentioned a very important one. It is going to create a certain amount of hardship in government work, and is something that should have been considered.
Industry all over the dominion has accepted the suggestions which have been put forward by the unions in this respect, but nurses and doctors who work in hospitals controlled by the government have no set time during which they shall work. They do not even have an 8-hour day. They are working on an extended program, and something along this line will be a Godsend to them. It is a very beneficial piece of legislation so far as they are concerned and will impose a further strain on the economy, whether it is the dominion government or the provincial government that is concerned because the hospitals are hard pressed now to get sufficient doctors and nurses.
If this bill becomes law, it will have a beneficial effect so far as they are concerned, there will have to be an arrangement under which they will get an 8-hour day and a 40-hour week in order to get the advantages which are long overdue. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre probably overlooked this. This is one of the benefits that will be derived from the statutory holidays, but it will also affect and be related to the 40-hour week.
There is also one other matter with regard to statutory holidays which is causing a little trouble in industry. When the statutory holiday falls on a Saturday the employees want Saturday to be considered as part of the week, and they want to get paid for that Saturday. Saturday has been a holiday down through the years. The employees have a 40-hour

Industrial Relations
week and therefore they do not get paid for Saturday when the holiday falls on that day. They have just lost it. One of the difficulties we find with a Saturday holiday and also a statutory holiday is that in our business, particularly, where we have to go on lots where there is a lot of car parking, we find that the only time we can get on is a Saturday or a statutory holiday because there are no cars on the lot at that time. That is the only time they will let you work there. You have to pay a man triple pay for a job that you find yourself legislated into because of the demands of the union.

I have heard the argument about the strain on the economy and the related arguments that employers use when discussing this question. But the hon. member has overlooked the fact that particularly when these matters are being negotiated between labour unions and employers they are in the final result written into an over-all package agreement that is the net result of negotiations. The principle of having pay for statutory holidays involves recognition of the fact that almost 100 per cent of those who are on wages and salaries do their budgeting from month to month and the fact statutory holidays may dislocate their budget has resulted in the wage bill being spread more evenly and including statutory holidays.
Again, the principle of punitive pay for statutory holidays is to prevent employers using the services of employees on a statutory holiday and while it is necessary for certain categories to remain at work the purpose is to ensure that no persons are required to work on a day considered to be either a religious or national holiday in order that they may be free to enjoy the holiday with the rest of their fellow citizens. The punitive aspect was introduced for that purpose.
The hon. member was concerned that the punitive measures might be too harsh when workers pay is doubled. If the pay is only doubled it simply means that the employer may work an employee on a statutory holiday and it costs him no more than to work him on any other day because he must pay him in any case for the statutory holiday should he remain at home. Therefore, to be consistent, double time or triple time are the only figures that may be used.
I have made some inquiries about legislation in the provinces. I find that in Saskatchewan this fact is recognized but they also provide there for the payment of double time and a half for certain employees who are not required to work because of the public service which they perform while those in performance of public service receive double time or straight time and a day off.

We talk and properly so; we talk about the rule of law and the rules of the house and say that they must be maintained. So they must and in my submission the government is seeking to maintain an elementary rule. But in addition to the rules written into the rule book, I have always understood that we are governed by the rule of common sense and that the rules of parliament are themselves based on common sense. It is a common sense rule that no private member should be allowed to move specific amendments with regard to the rates of taxation. That is an elementary protection to other private members. What kind of a position would you be in, Mr. Chairman, if that were allowed? I should go back a moment in order to anticipate an objection I know will be made.

Overruled the Chair.

We have a Speaker whom we all respect; we have chairmen who have given us what we consider to be fair rulings, and what have these people opposite done? They have undermined the Chair in this House of Commons at the very beginning of the first session of this parliament.

Mr. Chairman, I understand that the matter before the committee at present is a matter of order and that we have had decisions made by the chair on the point on two or three occasions within the last 48 hours. I understand further that those decisions have been in accordance with the practice of this house during the 25 sessions which I have attended and they have also been in accordance with the decisions made in 25 sessions of the legislature of the province which I attended before I came here. I have listened to some of the discussions earlier in this session and have even said to persons on this side of the house that the idea which has been expressed by the chairman of the committee in the last few days is in accordance with the long-time practice of an institution of this kind. That is, generally speaking, in dealing with matters having to do with money a private member has no right to stand up in his place and move for a further expenditure of money or for any action which might result in further expenditures of money, but he has a perfect right to get up and move that any expenditure of money which is proposed be cut down and reduced. Of course, one does not need to depend upon even the decisions of the chairmen in order to appreciate that that is true. I have here Hansard for July 26, 1956.
Now it is true it was the voting of money or the utilization of money that was under discussion, but the principle is the same no matter whether it has to do with that or whether it has to do with what we have been discussing. The present Minister of

It was on the basis of that principle, as I understand it, that decisions were given by the chairman in this committee within the last day or two. That is the matter which has been under discussion, and the committee has a perfect right to deal with a motion of that kind.

We have been discussing this question for some little time and I want to repeat that we have been twitted on this side of the house for not all being here in order to vote, and I want to say what has been repeated once or twice previously, that we had a very considerable number in the house, and if we had had a dozen more in the house it is true that the motion would not have carried-

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: You had them right behind the curtain.
And we could have brought them in and trimmed you to a frazzle.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.
Mr. Chairman-
Mr. Chairman, I am going to take only a few minutes-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.

Mr. Chairman, on a point of order, we have a right to be heard from this

corner of the house. You have heard a spokesman from the Liberal party and the C.C.F. party and I strongly object to your trying to shut off any debate from this corner of the house at this time.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I will listen to you.
Well, Mr. Chairman, I still have the floor.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I will ask the hon. member to discuss matters relevant to the discussion.

I am discussing matters
relevant to all that has been said here tonight.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I do not address that remark specifically to the hon. member for Melville. I am saying that to all hon. members.
It is a little late.

The matters that have been discussed in connection with this debate up to now are of course all relevant to the discussion which was permitted to take place and I think these things should be discussed to their logical conclusion. When hon. members opposite say to the group on this side of the house, "If you had had all your members in today we would have been defeated at this time," I must comment that I have never heard of a government wanting to be defeated in any house. Why did they want us to defeat them this afternoon?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The hon. member will understand that he is not discussing a matter relevant to the discussion.
The hon. member for Kamloops discussed the same question for ten minutes only a few moments ago.
That is right.

Since I am talking in favour of abiding by the Chairman's ruling I will accept his ruling and agree that, so long as he keeps the others in line in the same way in connection with this discussion I will have nothing more to say until we take the vote.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Thank you very much. The hon. member for Macleod.

Mr. Chairman, I am not going to take much time this evening but I do think a point should be covered here from this corner of the house. In speaking to the point of order may I just point out that there is quite a difference in the debate on this point of order today and the debate that we have heard take place on similar points of order during the last session of parliament. The difference is this: The Minister of Justice, when he sat on the other side of the house,
Income Tax Act
and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre seemed to be bosom pals.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: We still are.
They argued points of order much more intricate than this one and they were in 100 per cent agreement. The change of position appears to have changed their attitude.
You are bedfellows of the Liberals.

Let me proceed. The Minister of Justice rose a little while ago and said that members of the government challenged the Chairman's ruling because they thought the ruling was wrong. That is their privilege, of course, but I would like to know why they did not do that yesterday. That is a question I cannot resolve in the realm of common sense which my hon. friend the Minister of Justice has mentioned so frequently of late. Why was this not done yesterday? The arguments presented by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre this evening were the same arguments he raised yesterday and yet no protest was made at that time.
I want to compliment the Minister of Finance, however, on the way in which he handled this question yesterday. He rose in the house after the Chairman had made a ruling and explained that the government could not vote for the amendment, the reason being that if such an amendment were allowed to carry it would upset the balance of ways and means and it would only mean chaos as far as responsible government is concerned.
Now we have irresponsible government.

He explained that this was the way to look at it and so the government permitted the motion to be put and the motion was defeated on its merits. Why change the process today? Why change the process now?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Who
made the decision?

The same thing is happening now as happened yesterday. Why could the government not have permitted the motion to go before the house in the same way as the Minister of Finance permitted it to go before the house last night?
They are opposed to the amendment.

That would have been the solution to the problem; but no, they could not do that. I suspect they began to think the matter over and we can guess what it was they began to think over. They doubtless began to think that it was a bad political

Income Tax Act
move to let these motions be put before the house because someone would go out in the country and say, "The Conservatives voted against a reduction in taxation." That is what someone surely would have said and knowing this the government brought the Chair into what I claim to be disrespect and in doing this they have done the very thing they accused the previous administration of doing just a few months ago.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
As hon. members are aware, in this sitting on an appeal to the house from the decision of the Chairman of the committee of the whole this house decided that it was not in order for a private member to propose a reduction in taxation. As I am bound by that decision I must rule this amendment out of order for that reason. In due deference to the views expressed I do not believe I can ignore a decision of the house made in this regard earlier this day. I would like to quote Mr. Speaker Lemieux as recorded at page 632 of Beauchesne's third edition in these words:
The best authority for the Speaker is the judgment of the house. The Speaker merely voices the opinion of the house. The house, having declared out of order an amendment framed precisely as the one now under discussion, I am bound, in accordance with that decision and irrespective of the authorities, to rule the present motion also out of order.
Shall clause 3 carry?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, will the minister comment further with regard to the rates set by clause 3 for the purposes of the Income Tax Act? He will recall that I expressed approval of the way in which this reduction, if it was the only reduction that could be made, was to be put into effect in that it does not pyramid into the upper brackets, but specifically was consideration given to the proposition which hon. members of the government party advanced from time to time that the exemption levels should be increased, for example to $1,500 for a single person and $3,000 for a married person?
As the minister knows these exemption levels were established a long time ago. The cost of living has gone up a great deal since these levels were established. Is it not time that these levels were raised? We all recognize when we are discussing income tax that it is the fairest method of obtaining revenue from the people of the country but it is also the basic principle of income tax that you should not start taxing those dollars that are absolutely essential to an ordinary existence.
We claim that that is what is happening. We oppose income tax on income just over $1,000 for a single person and just over $2,000 for a married person. It seems to me that

is not a good substitute for the implementation of that other idea that the Conservatives have had. I should like to hear from the minister on this point.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the Prime Minister did not make any promise to the Canadian people in the campaign that if he were elected to office he would bring about a reduction in the tax through the medium of an increase of exemptions to $1,500 for single persons and $3,000 for married persons. Mr. Chairman, nothing would please the present Minister of Finance more than to be able to introduce responsibly such a proposal; but I come back to the point I have made already several times, that we were under very severe limitations coming into office now and having to function within the scope of an existing budget. The fact is, sir, that to put into effect an increase to $1,500 in the basic exemption for single persons and $3,000 for married persons would cost the treasury of this country approximately $530 million, and that kind of money was not available in the balance of ways and means within the scope of the budget that was passed at the last session of the house before dissolution.
Why did you say that during the election?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We did not say that.
You did, all over the country.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We talked about the overtaxation in the last fiscal year. The hon. member for Billingsgate knows that, he knows it very well. He should not go on mouthing things that he knows were applied to last year in the face of the huge overtaxation last year. I do not intend to be turned aside by those senseless interruptions of the hon. member.

On a question of privilege, sir, I am not sure whether the hon. gentleman was referring to me. If he was, he seems to have got the name of my constituency wrong. I would like to ask the hon. gentleman if he denies ever talking about $500 million surplus in the last election?
Overtaxation.
Overtaxation of half a billion dollars. Does he deny that?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I ask the hon member to stay with the matter under discussion.
He doesn't deny it.
Saved by the chair.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: May I proceed, Mr. Chairman? If the hon. member can just hold himself for only a moment he will get his answer.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I would ask the minister to discuss the matter before the chair.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That matter was discussed at the last session as applying to the last fiscal year, and a good deal was said about it, and a good deal more could be said about it yet.
Let me deal with the question raised by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, Mr. Chairman. I have pointed out what the proposal that he now inquires about would have cost in terms of loss of revenue to the treasury in a year and, faced with the limitations we were under, we looked about for a place where we thought reductions could be most effectively made. The conclusion we reached was that by concentrating our reduction on the income tax the two methods that would best achieve the concentration of the benefit of the reduction in income tax in favour of persons in the low income brackets were (a) an increase in the exemption now in respect of dependants; and (b) reductions in the rates in the lowest brackets of taxation.
That is why, Mr. Chairman, we have recommended to the house the reductions that appear in clause 3 of this bill, a reduction of two points from 13 per cent to 11 per cent on the first $1,000 of taxable income and a reduction of one point in the rate on the second $1,000 of taxable income. The net result of these two reductions is to reduce the load of income tax carried by the income taxpayers of Canada, 4J million of them, by $146 million in a full year.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have not kept a record-I have not the secretarial staff to keep this the way the Prime Minister can in regard to time spent on questions-of the number of times the Minister of Finance has pleaded that his government cannot do certain things because they are working within the framework of the budget of the former government.
Mr. Chairman, there are several facts about the clause that we are now discussing. First of all, it relates to the calendar year 1958 and to that period only. Nine months of that calendar year will be in a period presumably to be covered by a budget that may yet be brought in by this government. Even the first three months are the last three months of a period of more than nine months out of this fiscal year that this government will have been in office. This government, its
Income Tax Act
spokesmen, talked about the huge overtaxation, the huge surplus on the basis of which they would be able to implement their promises.
I have no defence of the former government, but it seems to me that this excuse has been worn thin, that the government has to keep telling us it cannot do the things it promised to do because of the limitations imposed upon it by Mr. Harris' budget. I repeat, these provisions are for the calendar year 1958, and if the Conservatives thought it was possible to do this kind of thing but now when they are on their own that they now find they cannot do them, why do they not honestly stand up and say they were wrong?
I recognize that even with such research as I have been able to carry on I have not been able to find a direct quotation that I can attribute to the Prime Minister to the effect that he would raise the exemption levels to $1,500 and $3,000. In fact, it is very interesting to go through the Prime Minister's speeches in the recent election campaign and see how he creates impressions, without putting things down in plain language. The Minister of Finance knows that in former years in this House of Commons in budget debates the members of the Progressive Conservative party did urge, and on occasion did move an amendment to the effect that the exemption levels should be raised. They created the impression, not just in the election campaign but across the years, that whereas the Liberals were stubborn and were unwilling to raise those exemption levels, the Conservatives would do it.
My contention is that clause 3, by the terms of subparagraph 2 thereof, relates to a period of time that is wholly within the control of this government. It relates to the calendar year 1958, the first three months of which are part of the present fiscal year and part of the nine months period that they will have been in office. The other nine months are entirely their own, if they are still there and if we do not have a change for the better in the meantime. In view of that, Mr. Chairman, the excuses given by the Minister of Finance are entirely inadequate.

Mr. Chairman, this unprecedented budget advanced in committee on the estimates of the minister to me, I think, brings to the attention of the house the desirability of following some recommendations that the minister himself made when he was sitting on this side, namely that of allowing members of parliament to meet and question officials of the government and examine the questions as to ways and means.

Income Tax Act
I am sure in my mind that the reason we have not got a white paper, as we should have at this time having regard to the big changes brought about by the new administration, is that the minister is advancing to the house his own off the cuff financial estimate. He is not prepared to advance a white paper that would have behind it the authority of the large number of people in the Bank of Canada, in his department, and elsewhere in whom the country has a great deal of confidence.
In the almost six months that the government has been in office circumstances have changed and, as I said in my remarks last Friday, they have changed for the worse. But based on the new declining levels of prosperity I think the Minister of Finance is not being frank with the house when he brings forward in an off the cuff speech last Friday night a statement of estimates of income and outgo involving millions and millions of dollars. I do not think these estimates have the imprimatur of the official level of government in this country in which we have had reason to have confidence.
In my opinion, this is a prime example if there ever was one of justification for referring the estimates of the department of the new minister to an estimates committee so that we could examine, as he himself has so often asked, some of the major economists and experts in the Department of Finance who could give us some idea as to the likely balance of ways and means as the result of some of these new proposals this session.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is not one word of truth in the charge just made by the hon. gentleman.

Would my hon. friend, in the knowledge that the session will continue after the new year, not agree that there might be some advantage in allowing the estimates committee to examine the whole set-up of ways and means in so far as our finances are concerned?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the hon. member never was more mixed up in his life than he is in the statement he just made. Never did anybody suggest that the estimates committee should do anything more than review estimates. He is talking now about an estimates committee that will review financial proposals in relation to taxation. The hon. member is completely mixed up. It is unfortunate.

Mr. Chairman, the Minister of Finance chose the introduction of his own estimates to offer the equivalent of a new budget and there was much complaint that the usual procedures, traditional for more

than 80 years, had not been utilized. I simply say to him, does that not justify more than ever directing to a committee of the house, and I think the estimates committee would be the proper one, estimates of the finance department so that we could have an opportunity to discuss with some of the senior officials of his department the opinions that they might have now as to the new levels of income and outgo of the government? No answer from the minister.

Mr. Chairman, earlier when the minister was discussing this clause he placed some emphasis on the idea that the intent of the government in these tax reduction proposals, even though he admitted they are relatively minor, was to give relief to those in the lower tax brackets. In view of the remarks he made about the limitations with which he was confronted in his efforts to reduce taxes, the question I should like to ask him relates to the fact that the reductions in taxes, as I understand the figures in the clause of the bill, carry through right up to the person whose taxable income is $400,000 a year or more.
The minister can correct me if I am wrong, but I think I am correct in suggesting that for the people whose taxable income amounts to more than $2,000 right up to those whose taxable income is $400,000 or more the tax reduction amounts to $30 a year. I remember somebody suggesting earlier in the debate today that $30 a year to the person who is in receipt of an income of $400,000 is a good deal smaller consideration than it is to the person who comes barely within the tax level as far as income is concerned.
Can the minister indicate to us what the total amount will be which he does not expect to receive as the result of carrying out the $30 reduction in the case of all those who have a taxable income above the level suggested in subsections (a) and (b)? Those are the two sections in the lower income tax group for which he is suggesting a special reduction in rate. Has he any figures which will indicate to the committee the loss of revenue to the treasury as the result of providing the $30 reduction from that point right through to those in the highest income brackets?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it would be an entirely new theory of progressive taxation to say that when you get above the level of $2,000 of taxable income you are not going to tax everybody in the same way on his initial $2,000 of taxable income. That would be an entirely new theory. You start everybody in the same way. The graduated rates apply to everybody and the reduction

is uniform as to amount. That is because we have started in the lowest brackets.
Ten o'clock.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the clause carry?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
No, ten o'clock.
Progress reported.

speechtext:
Can the hon. gentleman tell us what the business will be for tomorrow?
Business of the House Mr. Green: Mr. Speaker, tomorrow we shall commence with the bill having to do with the bridge over the Niagara. It was reported back from committee today. We will then continue with the debate on the amendments to the Income Tax Act; then we will take the Export Credits Insurance Act; then the resolution dealing with guaranteed prices for agricultural commodities; and then the estimates of the Department of Justice.
